speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY INTO CONDUCT AND CERTAIN ALLEGED STATEMENTS
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Justice, in view of many and strong statements which have appeared in the press, whether it is true that an investigation has been ordered to be held against His Honour Judge Stubbs of the county court of Manitoba with respect to certain statements made by him, and if so, what is the nature of the investigation, and is the investigation being proceeded with?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INQUIRY INTO CONDUCT AND CERTAIN ALLEGED STATEMENTS
speechtext:
While I have not the file before me I think I can speak from memory in reply to the question. As my hon. friend is aware, for some time back complaints have been received in the Department of Justice in regard to the conduct of Judge Stubbs, who for some time occupied not only the position of judge of the county court in the province of Manitoba, but also judge of the surrogate court of that province. I find on the file, before this government came into office, that complaints reached the department, but that no action apparently was taken in regard to them. Shortly after I became Minister of Justice a complaint was received from the attorney general of the province of Manitoba, who is the head of the administration of law in that province. If my memory serves me aright, that was in January, 1931. When the complaint was received from such a responsible authority in the province I felt it my duty to
consult Judge Stubbs in regard to the charges which were made. A letter was sent to him and I received a reply from him to the effect that he had been misreported in the Winnipeg newspapers, and that any remarks of his did not bear the interpretation which the newspapers placed upon them. No action was taken in regard to that complaint.
Subsequently another complaint was received, I think signed by all or nearly all the members of the superior court of the province of Manitoba, in regard to certain language which had been used by Judge Stubbs seriously reflecting upon the judges of the court of appeal of that province. In regard to that complaint Judge Stubbs took the objection that in anything he had said on the bench he was speaking merely as a judge of the surrogate court of the province of Manitoba and that as judges of the surrogate courts of the various provinces are appointed, not by this government, but by provincial governments, he contended that this department had no right to make any inquiry or offer any objection to anything which he might have said as judge of the surrogate court of the province of Manitoba, although I am free to admit to the house that the language of Judge Stubbs in that particular instance was somewhat extreme and very condemnatory of the superior court judges of the province of Manitoba. No action, therefore, was taken with regard to that complaint.
More recently, within the last month or six weeks, a further complaint and a very definite one was made by the attorney general of the province of Manitoba, stating that the language and the conduct of Judge Stubbs was bringing the administration of justice in the province of Manitoba into disrepute. Upon receipt of so formidable a protest from the constituted authorities in the province of Manitoba I thought it was my duty to order an investigation, and accordingly I recommended that a commission should issue for the purpose of inquiring into the conduct of Judge Stubbs. A commission was subsequently issued and the Hon. Mr. Justice Ford of the court of appeal of the province of Alberta was appointed commissioner. I believe that the commissioner will proceed with the investigation. Counsel has been appointed to assist the commissioner by bringing all the evidence before him, and express instructions have been given to counsel that he is to act in his capacity as assistant to the commissioner for the purpose of submitting evidence, not in any sense of the word as a prosecuting attorney, but to see that all the evidence is submitted, and for that pur-

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, October 12, consideration of the motion of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett (Prime Minister) for approval of the trade agreement entered into at Ottawa the 20th day of August, 1932, between representatives of His Majesty's government in Canada and of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the fiscal changes consequent thereto.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the motion which is before the house reads as follows:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the trade agreement entered into at Ottawa the 20th day of August, 1932, between representatives of His Majesty's government in Canada and of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the fiscal changes consequent thereto.
The agreement will be found in the supplementary volume, which is annex V. tabled a day or two ago by the right hon. the Prime

Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
Minister. The agreement itself covers three pages of the report, pages 50 to 52 inclusive, and the schedule setting forth the proposed changes in the customs tariff occupies pages 53 to 67 inclusive. The agreement should be read, I think, in the light of the speech made by the right hon. the Prime Minister at the time of presenting to the house the motion for its approval.
The agreement is one intended to increase trade between Canada and Great Britain, and to do so by means of imperial preferences. The preferences being the main feature of the agreement it might be advisable to say a word or two at the cutset as to the history of the imperial preference, so called.
As is known, the imperial preference, or as it was first called, the British preference, had its origin in a resolution and action by this parliament of Canada. That I am sure should foe a source of pride to Canadians wholly irrespective of the party to which they may belcng. It is a source of especial pride to the Liberal party that the resolution respecting the British preference was introduced into this parliament at the instance of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the leader of a Liberal administration, and his illustrious Minister of Finance of that day, Right Hon. W. S. Fielding. The preference, in a word, as it relates to the customs tariff, is simply a means whereby there is given to the country to which the preference is accorded, the right to have its commodities enter the country according the preference at a rate of duty lesser than that imposed against countries generally. The British preference as introduced in 1897 provided that goods coming from Great Britain should enter this country at a rate of 124 per cent lower than that prevailing generally. In the following year the 124 per cent was increased to 25 per cent, and in the year 1900 the British preference reached 33-j per cent.
From that period on, with the exception of a time during the war, when, on one occasion, there was some decrease in the preference, there have been changes made to effect increases in the British preference. From time to time an increasing number of commodities have been placed on the free list, and under the preference with respect to a very considerable number there has been accorded further increases. The most important changes in the British preference of recent years were prior to the time the present administration took office. They were made in the year 1930. At that time the changes became effective under what has come to be termed the Dunning budget, a
budget introduced in this house by the Hon. Charles Dunning, the then Minister of Finance. That budget made provision for considerable increases in the British preference. At that time a very large number of additional commodities were placed upon the free list, and on others the preference in favour of Great Britain was made very much greater than it had been at any previous time.
I should mention at this point that within two years after the late Liberal administration came into office, we took another step which still further increased the preference in favour of Great Britain. In 1923 we secured an enactment whereby a discount of ten per cent on preference rates was given where goods were brought into Canada through Canadian ports. It was ascertained at the time that 99 per cent of the goods coming from British countries into Canada came through Canadian ports, with the additional ten per cent practically all goods came into Canada in that way.
In these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, there can be no doubt in the mind of any one as to where the official opposition or, to put it in another way, the Liberal party in Canada, stands on the matter of British preference. We were the originators of the British preference; we have maintained it against the opposition of hon. gentlemen opposite, and we have done more than all other parties combined to make the British preference a success.
In speaking a few days ago, my right hon. friend sought to have the house believe that in the matter of his so-called imperial preferences he was following in the footsteps of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and that what he now claims to have accomplished is something which Sir Wilfrid Laurier failed to accomplish, although he had made an attempt so to do. My right hon. friend made a similar statement last year. How he can so assert, in the face of the facts, is more than I can understand. At this time I believe it my duty to make clear to the house the grounds upon which he seeks to base his assertion. Perhaps I should do my right hon. friend most justice if I read his statement as presented to this house a few days ago. He said:
In addressing the house on April 26 last I placed on Hansard extracts from the memorandum submitted by Sir Wilfrid Laurier to the British government at the Colonial conference of 1902. It was at that time, you will recall, that Sir Wilfrid Laurier, ceasing



Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
to agree with his delegate colleagues, took a very definite stand with respect to imperial preference. Let me requote from the memorandum this paragraph so apposite to the discussions on this subject today:
The quotation is as follows:
The Canadian ministers stated that if they could be assured that the Imperial government would accept the principle of preferential trade generally, and particularly grant to the tood products of Canada in the United Kingdom exemption from duties now levied, or hereafter imposed, they, the Canadian ministers, would be prepared to go further into the subject and endeavour to give to the British manufacturer some increased advantage over his foreign competitors in the markets of Canada.
Then the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) continues:
I now only ask, and I sincerely hope that the parliament of Canada, now seeing accomplished the task which was attempted by that distinguished leader of the party which now sits to the left of the Speaker, can with one voice, approve the agreements which nothing but mutual trust and confidence, mutual hope and the common appreciation of the fundamental principles on which empire business should be conducted, could have brought about.
What are the facts as to the circumstances to which the paragraph quoted owed its origin? After the South African war additional expenditures had to be met by the government of Great Britain, and to meet those expenditures, a slight tax on wheat from all countries was imposed by the British government for revenue purposes. The tax was a duty of three pence per hundred weight on wheat imported from all sources. That tax appeared in the budget of 1902, the year of the conference in England. I ask the house to take note of the fact that the British government had imposed a tax for revenue purposes before the conference met, a duty was in effect at the time the Canadian ministers were meeting in London. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Canadian ministers asked that the duty, in so far as it applied to Canada, should be reduced or removed. I repeat; they asked that the duty should be reduced or removed. When my right hon. friend went to England in 1930, he did not ask that duties should be reduced or removed, he asked that the British government should change entirely its fiscal policy and impose duties where no duties formerly existed. He asked that Great Britain should impose duties in order that a preference might thereby be granted. That is a wholly different course of procedure and a preference of an entirely different kind.
May I say that up until the time the present Prime Minister of Canada made his demand in 1930 on the British government- rvhich, as I have already described was, to all intents and purposes, a demand that the British government should change its fiscal policy, should become a protectionist administration, should impose protective tariffs in order to grant preferences-until that time no one of whom I am aware in any parliament of the British Empire ever formally suggested that a preference should be given by way of increasing tariffs rather than decreasing them. So that there is the fundamental difference which must be kept in mind when we compare the action of the recent Imperial economic conference at Ottawa, and any action previously taken concerning preferences. The difference is one founded on the different points of view of the great political parties with respect to trade policies generally.
The Liberal party has always advocated greater freedom of trade. When it has advocated a tariff, it has been a tariff for revenue, protection being only incidental. The Liberal party has never advocated protection. Hon. gentlemen opposite have always advocated a policy of protection,

of course, I am speaking of the recent past. Their policy with respect to trade matters has been wholly protectionist, and the difference between the two parties on tariff questions lies .in their different points of view as to what they believe to be in the interests of the country, so far as trade and fiscal matters are concerned. The preferences of the present Conservative party have been given in the main by increasing tariffs and thereby applying the policy of protection, whereas the Liberal preferences have always been along the lines of reducing rather than increasing duties. On all occasions Sir Wilfrid Laurier made it very clear that the last thing he would ever think of in seeking a preference from another country of the British Empire would be to interfere in the domestic affairs of that country or to ask its government to alter its fiscal policy, let alone seek to compel it so to do. Therein lies the fundamental difference between the methods which have been adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite to bring about the agreement we now have before us, and anything that has hitherto prevailed in British history with respect to the granting of a preference to or by the mother country. Let me read what the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said in this House of Commons on March 27, 1907, which makes wholly clear what his view was with regard to any preference which a government might seek to obtain from the

United Kingdom
British government by compelling it to alter its fiscal policy. I read from page 5538 of Hansard for 1907:
We would not accept the idea that the British public should force upon us their own fiscal views and no more would they tolerate the idea that we should force upon them our own fiscal views, and therefore the only way in which the British Empire can be maintained upon its present foundation is by allowing to every nation composing it the measure of liberty that it has and also the free choice of the fiscal policy which it is to maintain.
That was not a view taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier only; it has been adopted by every prime minister of Canada, with the exception of my right hon. friend. The Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald took that view very strongly at the beginning of his great political career in Canada; this is the view that was taken by Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden during the time he was in office, and this is the view to which Right Hon. Arthur Meighen adhered while in office in any legislation which came before the house on the subject of preferences. Let me give hon. gentlemen opposite Sir John A. Macdonald's view with regard to this question of seeking to effect a preference by compelling another part of the empire to alter its tariffs. Conditions have changed very considerably since those early days. The difficulty then was not with the young dominions trying to force the hand of the mother country; it arose through the attempt on the part of the mother country to restrain the dominions in the matter of their freedom. Even prior to confederation Sir John A. Macdonald, who headed the administration in office at the time, instructed * Sir Alexander Galt, his then Minister of Finance, to inform the British ministry by means of an official despatch of what was the position of the Conservative party in Canada and of Canada itself with respect to matters of the kind. Here is a part of the communication which was sent in 1859 by Sir Alexander Galt to His Grace the Duke of Newcastle, who at that time was Colonial Secretary:
Respect to the Imperial government must always dictate the desire to satisfy them that the policy of this country is neither hastily nor unwisely formed; and that due regard is had to the interests of the mother country as well as of the province. But the government of Canada, acting for its legislature and people, cannot, through those feelings of deference which they owe to the Imperial authorities. in any manner waive or diminish the right of the people of Canada to decide for themselves both as to the mode and extent to which taxation shall be imposed. Self government would be utterly annihilated if the view

of the Imperial government were to be preferred to those of the people of Canada. It is, therefore, the duty of the present government distinctly to affirm the right of the Canadian legislature to adjust the taxation of the people in the way they deem best, even if it should unfortunately happen to meet with the disapproval of the Imperial ministry.
That statement was made by Sir John A. Macdonald's government as long ago as 1859. As to the views of Sir Robert Borden, let me quote very briefly from a statement which appears in the London Times of August 1, 1918, in reference to a statement made by Sir Robert at the Savoy hotel, London, on July 31, 1918:
As Canada claimed and exercised the right absolutely to control her own fiscal policy, Sir Robert said, so the representatives of the dominions necessarily refrained from attempting any interference in the fiscal policy of the United Kingdom.
Moreover, the people of Canada would not desire the people of the United Kingdom to shape or modify their fiscal policy solely to give a preference to the products of Canada, especially if such change should involve any supposed injustice, or should be regarded as unfair or oppressive by a considerable portion of the people of the United Kingdom.
In view of what we already know as to the manner in which the agreement is being received by a considerable portion of the people of the United Kingdom, Mr. Speaker, I think I should repeat that paragraph for the careful consideration of hon. members of the house:
Moreover, the people of Canada would not desire the people of the United Kingdom to shape or modify their fiscal policy solely to give a preference to the products of Canada, especially if such change should involve any supposed injustice, or should be regarded as unfair or oppressive by a considerable portion of the people of the United Kingdom.
On his return to Canada, Sir Robert is reported in the Toronto Globe of September 3, 1918, as having said:
We hold ourselves free to work out the problem of preference according to Canadian needs and conditions. For the same reason Canada must avoid any attempt at interference with the domestic policy of Great Britain.
Those views were held consistently, as I have said, by all prime ministers and I think by all political parties in this country until my right hon. friend took the opposite attitude at the conference of 1930. There have been other economic conferences, and at each one those who represented Canada have taken a position in accordance with the policies that I have indicated in the extracts I have read.
May I say that there is everything to be said in favour of conferences between the heads of the governments of the different parts

of the British Empire. It is well that those who represent the different parts of the empire should meet together periodically and discuss matters of mutual and common interest. Out of discussions of that kind, which help to acquaint each part with the difficulties experienced in other parts, and which help indicate lines that can be followed in order to further mutual interests, there is bound to come to the respective governments the line which can be followed with the greatest certainty of achieving not only in the short run but in the long run as well the object that is to be attained.
In 1923 there were two conferences in London held simultaneously, one the Imperial conference, so-called, and the other the Imperial economic conference. At the Imperial economic conference Canada was represented by the late Sir Lomer Gouin and the Right Hon. George P. Graham, and as the one holding the office of Prime Minister at the time, I was also present at both conferences and participated in the proceedings though more particularly in those of the Imperial conference. At the economic conference in London we were asked by the British government whether we desired to have preferences granted by means of the raising of the British tariff. A Conservative government was in office in Great Britain, headed by the Right Hen. Stanley Baldwin, and the Right Hon. Neville Chamberlain was Chancellor of the Exchequer, while the Right Hon. Sir Philip Cunliffe-Lister was minister of one of the departments at the time.

Yes. These
gentlemen were most prominent in the affairs of the conference on the British side so far as economic questions were concerned. As I say, we were asked whether Canada desired preferences to be given by an increase in the tariff in Great Britain against other countries in such a manner as would permit of such preferences being granted to us. Our reply was that while Canada would always appreciate any preference which the mother country might wish to extend in the rate of duties on commodities going from this country into the old land, it was for Great Britain herself to decide what her own fiscal policy should be. We said that we would not undertake to say to Britain that she must change her fiscal policy; we would not make a demand on her that she should place duties on the food of the people as a means of reciprocating what Canada had done. We claimed that what Canada

had done with respect to preferences had been done for the sake of this country quite as well as for the sake of the empire. Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to forget that. They talk about concessions; but after all what was the governing principle with respect to preferences when they were granted? Were the preferential rates introduced and maintained by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and afterwards maintained by the government of Sir Robert Borden, and, later, by that of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, simply for the purpose of helping the mother country? Undoubtedly it was hoped that the preferences granted would help the mother country; but above all it was believed that they would be of special benefit to this country, and it was for that reason that the preference was initiated and maintained. There was mutual benefit. Hon. gentlemen opposite talk as though trade were a matter of war, in which one side must be victor and the other vanquished. As a matter of fact, there would be no trade at all unless there were mutual advantage as a result thereof; because people would not join even for exchange except upon that principle.
Now, the benefit, so far as Canada is concerned, has been great to the large body of her consumers; it has afforded reasonable competition, and has helped to keep down the cost of living in the necessaries of life as well as in many other important articles. But there is another benefit, and it is an allimportant one so far as Canada as a whole is concerned, and that is the benefit which accrues from a decrease in the cost of production, particularly as affecting those engaged in the great basic industries of mining, lumbering, fishing and agriculture in this vast land. Unless costs of production are kept down, how are our great basic industries going to compete successfully in the markets of the world that lie beyond our own shores? It has been for these reasons, therefore, that the preference has been granted in the past, and for this further reason. It has been and must be apparent that no country can go on trading all the time in one direction; it must be Obvious that transportation costs alone, which enter so largely into what we buy and what we can sell, will be kept down only as vessels are kept carrying goods in both directions. But in a larger way still, it must be apparent that sooner or later exports must be paid for by imports. In this regard, I am glad to see that the right hon. the Prime Minister the other day went so far as to admit that fact. For the first time, I think, it has

United Kingdom
been admitted by hon. gentlemen opposite. This is what the right hon. gentleman said: For we must commonly agree that there can be no continued sale without purchase; that if we expect to market our goods in the United Kingdom we must expect to purchase goods from the United Kingdom.
There at last we have a straightforward admission from the government that exports are paid for by imports. And what is true of trade between the United Kingdom and Canada is equally true of trade between other parts of the world and this country.
It has been on that basis that in the past this country has favoured the British preference in the manner I have described. It was a means of increasing trade, and if hon. gentlemen opposite want any assurances as to how successfully it worked, particularly when administered by a Liberal administration,
I ask them to look at the record of trade under the government of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and under the recent Liberal administration in Canada. They will see just what the figures are.
But to return to the conference of 1923. As I have said, when the British ministers inquired whether we wished to have duties imposed, and we replied it was for the British government itself to decide what duties it might wish to impose, we were met next with the question: Will you give us a list of the articles on which it would be most helpful to Canada to have an increase in the event of our deciding for ourselves to place duties against other countries with respect to certain commodities? In other words, they were adopting the method which one would hope would always be adapted at imperial conferences, namely, of seeking to ascertain from all sides what was going to be of the greatest benefit all round. I need not discuss the answer that was made to that question. There was tabled in this house in 1924 sessional paper No. Ill, which contains the correspondence which took place between myself and members of the British government with respect to the preference; and the Right Hon. Mr. Graham made a statement in this house in 1924 in which he reviewed at considerable length the action taken by Canada's ministers at the economic conference of the previous year.
We gave to the British ministry a list of the commodities on which we believed it would be to Canada's advantage to have a preference in the manner suggested provided Great Britain, on her own account, decided to alter her fiscal system, and to impose duties. We pointed out the particular articles on which
in our opinion it would be of special advantage to Canada, in that event, to have a preference granted. The result was that before the conference was over the British ministry presented to the conference a statement to the effect that they intended to invite His Majesty's government to impose duties with respect to a number of commodities which we had mentioned to them, and which were on the list we had submitted. I have in my hand a summary of the conclusions of the Imperial economic conference of 1923, and I find on page 4 the following:
Further, as regards imperial preference under the United Kingdom customs tariff to empire goods. His Majesty's government intimated that they intended to submit to parliament the following proposals:
I will not read the proposals, but they referred to dried fruit, currants, other dried fruit, other preserved fruits, sugar, tobacco, wine, raw apples, canned salmon and canned lobster, crayfish, and crabs, honey, lime, lemon and other fruit juices. There was a considerable number of commodities on which the British government itself undertook at that conference to grant a preference, provided the parliament of Great Britain were prepared to implement their action in that regard. If hon. gentlemen opposite will compare this list with what has been presented to us in the report tabled by my right hon. friend, they will find that the preferences which have been granted at this time are in very considerable part the same or similar to what was obtained voluntarily in 1923.

My right hon. friend says "obtained". I am glad he has thus interrupted me. Yes, obtained, so far as the conference is concerned, and that is all my right hon. friend can now say with regard to the conference of 1932. I want the house to take very careful note of this, because it again touches something that is a matter of fundamental difference between my right hon. friend and myself. My right hon. friend would have us believe that because the British people at an election held subsequently to the conference refused to endorse a protectionist policy in Britain, Canada in 1923 failed to obtain what she has now, without any opportunity being afforded the British people to say whether or not they approve of what it is alleged has been obtained. I submit there is a difference that reaches to the very roots of all that pertains to the maintenance of friendly relations between different governments of the empire. Only as a government acts in accordance with the will of its parlia-

ment, as that will is representative of the will of the people, can it be said that any agreement that is arrived at between two parts of the empire is on a basis which is either worth while or likely to prove enduring. The conference of 1923 obtained, as I have said, the particular concessions, if you wish to refer to the matter in that way, voluntarily from the British government; but after the conference was over, Mr. Baldwin and his government decided to appeal to the people and they appealed in part on this protectionist program. What was the result? The result was that the electorate of Britain swept Mr. Baldwin and his administration out of office and returned another government. Fortunately there could be no unfavourable reaction so far as Canada was concerned. There had been no compulsion on our part; no attempt to compel the British government to accept any protectionist proposal of ours. The British government did what it did of its own volition, did it in a way it believed was going to be helpful, but in accordance with protectionist policies which were not acceptable to the people of Britain. When Mr. Ramsay MacDonald's government was returned, Mr. MacDonald assumed a very broad attitude on the matter in parliament, notwithstanding the fact that he had come into office in part in opposition to what had been put forward by the Conservative government of the day with respect to what had been done at the Imperial economic conference. Mr. Ramsay MacDonald said: I will present to parliament this undertaking in so far as it relates to what was promised with respect to the increase of duties at the Imperial conference, and I will allow members to vote as they please on the general items. I shall not expect my followers to support them or to oppose them. Every member of the house is free to vote as he pleases. The vote was taken and was against putting into effect those increased duties upon the food of the people of Great Britain. There the matter rested. If hon. gentlemen opposite are going to claim that they have won something that was not won in 1923, because in 1923 the people were allowed a voice as to whether or not they should be taxed on their food, whereas the matter to-day is being put through in a way which will prevent anything of that kind, then they are taking a course that is very dangerous not only for this country and for the old country, but for the future of the British Empire as a whole. It is on that ground, above every other, that I say to my right hon. friend at this moment, that before tariff schedules are changed in a manner which is going to impose increased duties

generally on the people of Canada, and increased duties in the way of taxes on food upon the people of Great Britain, the people of Canada and Great Britain should have a right to express their views with regard to the matter.
Oh, oh.

Who is telling Great
Britain now what she should do?

Hon. gentlemen opposite hoot at the idea of allowing the people to have a say as to whether or not they shall be taxed. That is typically Tory. I repeat that no executive has a right to bind a nation in any matter seriously affecting its fiscal policy without the consent of the people of that nation. I shall not take more time with reference to the conference of 1923.
Let me come now to the conference of 1930. Why was the conference of 1930 the failure it was? Hon. gentlemen opposite are beginning to say that the failure was deliberate, that the conference was intended so to be made by the Prime Minister and they are giving credit to the Prime Minister for his statesmanship in that regard. It was the failure that it was, because, as I said, for the first time in British history the Prime Minister of one of the dominions went to an Imperial conference and told the members of the British government that so far as his country was concerned there would be no negotiations with the British government unless they changed their fiscal policy; that only on the basis of the British government increasing duties in a manner which would enable preferences to be brought about through an increase in duties in the old land, would Canada be prepared to negotiate. Well, Britain was not at that time prepared to change her fiscal policy. The principle was fundamental in the minds of the Britishers of the day that above all they would be masters in their own household and would decide for themselves what fiscal policy they wished to have. It is true the fiscal policy of Britain has been changed since that date, but that does not alter the principle as to whether one part of the empire is to have the right to interfere in the affairs of another with a view to occasioning or actually forcing a change of fiscal policy. Well, to put the matter bluntly, hon. gentlemen opposite say that it is due to the Prime Minister of Canada that Britain's fiscal policy was changed in 1930. Some of them said so the other day, but on reflection they are a little quieter today than they were last week. If the Prime

United Kingdom
Minister of Canada is responsible for Great Britain introducing protectionist policies, I hope those of his followers who come from rural constituencies and who support the Prime Minister will give a little consideration to what may be the fate of the farmers in this country when the farmers of the old country begin to demand protection against the dominions as well as foreign countries in respect to their products, in virtue of a protectionist policy having been put into force in Great Britain.
Let me contrast what was done in 1930 as to method and as to proposals with what was done as the last act of the late Liberal administration. The act of the late Liberal administration in preparing for the conference in 1930 was to make it apparent to the people of Great Britain that we wished and were prepared to trade with them by giving them a very liberal increase in British preference; that in order to further trade within the Empire we were prepared to divert to Great Britain trade from those countries that were not prepared to trade on equally favourable terms with us, and that we were prepared to do all this first of all because we believed it was in our interest to do it, 'but also because we believed it would be in the interest of Great Britain and of the British Empire as well. There can be no question as to where the Liberal party stands in its desire to trade with the countries of the British Empire and the United Kingdom in particular. All that the Liberal party has to do is to point to its record. It has a record that has never been surpassed by any government with respect to what it evidences of a desire to further inter-imperial trade. More than that, we sought to make it perfectly clear that in what we were doing we were respecting above all else the fiscal autonomy of all parts of the empire. We were making it clear to Great Britain, as the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin sought to make it clear in this chamber in his first speech at the recent conference, that after all it was a great thing to have the goodwill of the mother country, to have the great market which she was giving us free from customs duties; that that was something which Canada had been receiving, and about which there had not been any bargaining. We equally were seeking to make clear our belief that on the basis of goodwill and common interest we were likely to get much further than on any bargaining basis. There is just that difference in the two methods. The one method found expression in what was said by Mr. Dunning at the conclusion of his budget speech. I will read his
words and by way of contrast with the other method quote the words of another, one highly thought of throughout the Empire, who has given his estimate of what bargaining means. Hon. Mr. Dunning, speaking in this house, May 1, 1930, said:
These tariff favours to those who favour our products are not the result of any bargain with any other country but of an attitude in international relations which we believe to be mutually beneficial and are an expression of the spirit in which Canada will approach the Imperial economic conference in a few months' time. In other words we do not intend to meet the other countries of the British commonwealth of nations in a spirit of petty bargaining but rather in the broad spirit of willingness to become in ever-increasing measure good customers to those who treat us in like manner. This is the spirit in which we desire to meet all nations, but we believe that within the British community of nations lies the greatest measure of opportunity for mutual development of trade because of our common heritage, kindred institutions and a common patriotism.
We had a visit last year from Sir Josiah Stamp, and we were told from more quarters than one that Sir Josiah Stamp's opinion on imperial questions was one to which heed should be given.

Let me read the words given to the Canadian people at the time Sir Josiah Stamp was here:
Instead of uniting the different parts of the empire, the bargaining process, bound up as it is with methods of blasting and blockading, will serve to disrupt and dismember the enipire as nothing which has occurred since its inception.
There, Mr. Speaker, you have what may be said of the two methods, the one of voluntary concession arrived at as the result of negotiation, aiming to discover what is of mutual interest and mutual benefit, and which makes its appeal to all that is highest and best in human nature; and the other the method of blasting and blockading, the essence of the bargaining method, appealing as it does to the hardest instincts in human nature.
In order that there may be no mistake as to where the Liberal party stands on the matter of the preference, may I repeat here what I said in South Huron, and what I have said repeatedly at other times and in other localities, that the policy of the Liberal party with respect to trade is to encourage greater freedom of trade, to remove restrictions and barriers rather than to increase them, and that if as a party we were returned to office our first objective would be to bring the tariff of Canada back to where it was ait the time we went out of office.

May I go a step further and say in connection with that, so that there can be no mistake as to where we stand in the matter of British trade, and the British preference, that we would undertake to give to the trade of the United Kingdom, where goods are imported through Canadian ports, a British preference averaging fifty per cent of our general tariff. If there is anything in this particular agreement that is comparable to that of advantage to ourselves and to British peoples in trade, I hope we will find it out before this discussion is over.
I say that in an attitude of that kind which favours the free flow of trade, without restrictions or barriers, in known and definite channels, subject to known and definite rates of duty, there is an opportunity for a country to build up its business and to go ahead in its relations with other parts of the empire. But under the bargaining business, under agreements such as have been arrived at here, what do we get? First we get locked agreements which are difficult to administer, which are very hard to understand, which can only be understood after they are interpreted; and which when interpreted depend for adherence to the interpretation given on those who are entrusted with their administration. If trade between one part of the empire and another is of any advantage in itself, why should not that trade flow in free and unchecked channels instead of being transferred by the terms of locked agreements which tend to impede its course all along the way? It is a more costly method, the locked agreement method; it is more uncertain, it begets disagreements and gives rise to feelings of distrust and discord which happily the other method wholly and successfully avoids.
Having said what I have with respect to the position of the Liberal party on the matter of imperial preference, may I say just a word to my right hon. friend about the attitude of the Liberal party towards himself and his government since he has come into office and in particular towards the recent economic conference. I did not expect my right hon. friend to be either gracious or chivalrous in his attitude towards me and towards the Liberal party, but I hardly expected him to go the length he went the other day in his remarks, when referring to myself, he said to this house:
There was nothing he could do to injure that conference that he did not do before it was held. There was no platform upon which he appeared that he did not endeavour in some way to make it more difficult for the government of his country to represent Canada at that conference.
Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen opposite are only following their leader in saying "hear, hear", But may I say, and I speak now in view of the people of Canada as a whole, that if any government in the world was ever given a free hand by an opposition from the time it came into office until the present, hon. gentlemen opposite have had that free hand. If there has been any exception taken to the course now adopted by some of my own supporters, it has been that I have refrained so completely between sessions from going from one end of the country to the other attacking the present administration. May I say that prior to the conference of 1930, in the short session that was held here, the government were allowed the right of wray in the legislation the.v brought in, without any opposition at all. All their tariff changes were put through without any pretence at criticism on the part of hon. gentlemen on this side. When my right hon. friend was at the Imperial conference, in London in 1930, great as was the temptation to have the British people feel that his course certainly was not representative of Canada's methods, I said nothing, I remained silent, and when, in the other sessions we have had here, dealing with the question of unemployment and the like, while we have had to register our disapproval of his methods and policies, it cannot be said that we have sought to embarrass the Prime Minister. And particularly with regard to this recent Imperial conference may I say that, if hon. gentlemen opposite will read what I said in this house before the conference took place, they will find that it corresponds in all particulars with what I am saying to-day. I pointed out what I feared would be the inevitable consequence of a certain course of procedure in many particulars that have since become so evident. Outside of this parliament I made no speech in respect to the conference except where it was absolutely necessary for me to do so as a result of action of hon. gentlemen opposite. While I am referring to this subject may I on behalf of the Canadian people extend to the people of Great Britain an apology on behalf of this country for language on the part of its Prime Minister which would infer that those who have dared to venture to take exception to features of the agreement which has been arrived at in this city are lacking in patriotism and loyalty to the empire. Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen opposite say, "hear, hear." so there can be no doubt on that score. Now I ask the house to

listen to the statement of principle underlying these agreements as given by the Prime Minister. At page 109 of Hansard of October 12, 1932, he is reported as having said:
These agreements mark the first forward step in a definite scheme of closer empire economic association. They are based upon the principle enunciated by the Conservative party before the last general election, and steadfastly supported by it from that time to the present. I made it clear that in our opinion the ideal application of the principle of protection involved an equalization of benefits thereunder as between manufactured and natural products.
And again:
Nor at this time do I wish to point the moral and suggest that the policies of this government, those which throughout the long years the party it represents has so unswervingly supported, must inevitably be the only policies on which a mutually beneficial plan of empire trade could be developed.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, how in the face of those statements are hon. members on this side of the house who have been opposed to the principle of protection as enunciated by hon. gentlemen opposite, to be expected to support the agreements now before us? How can we be expected to support them, and still preserve our self-respect in the matter of supporting our own principles? The Prime Minister has said: "They are based upon the principle enunciated by the Conservative party before the last general election." What was the principle of which he speaks?
The national convention held in Winnipeg on October 10 to 12, 1927, affirmed its adherence to the principle of the historic fiscal policy of the Conservative party. It is true that hon. gentlemen opposite ran away from the word "protection." They were afraid to use that word openly in the west, but every one knows what the historic fiscal policy of hon. gentlemen opposite is. It is the old Tory policy of protection. Under the present administration, however, it has become a policy of very high protection, a protection amounting almost to prohibition; in fact, in the great majority of cases it does amount to prohibition.
So I ask, Mr. Speaker: how are those of us who fought the Conservative policy in the election campaign of 1930, who have based our policies not on increases but on lowering of tariffs, and have made our appeal to the people on that score-how are we to support a trade agreement which the Prime Minister tells us is based on that principle? hon. gentleman opposite has made it impossible for us, even if we wished to do so, to support these agreements in their entirety. My right hon. friend goes a step farther and makes his position doubly clear, by stating, "They conform to the general plan proposed by this government at the economic conference held in London two years ago." What was that general plan? The plan was that the British government was to change its fiscal policy, that it was to become a protectionist government, and that only when it became protectionist would the government of Canada undertake to deal with it in the matter of reciprocal tariffs. My right hon. friend said, "We do not want any preferences granted by the lowering of tariffs, but what we tell you you must do is this: you must increase tariffs by 10 per cent." He went a step further at the conference and said, "I am appealing to you on the basis upon which the Conservative party in Canada appealed to the country in the general election of 1930. I am here representing a Canada first policy, and that Canada first policy means that nothing which can be produced or manufactured in Canada shall be permitted to come into Canada except over tariff walls high enough to keep out anything in the nature of effective competition." That was the doctrine as he laid it down; there can be no mistake. Let me read what my right hon. friend said in London.
The Conservative party of Canada believes in and employs the principle of protection of the home producer of agricultural and fabricated products from harmful interference or world competitors. This policy of the Conservative party has come to be known as the policy of Canada-first. In approaching the economic problems of our empire, I stand foursquare behind that policy. And if this conference is to meet these problems, and provide an effective solution of them, it seems to me my attitude towards my own country will be the attitude of you all towards yours. On no other basis can we hope to effect an enduring agreement of benefit to each one of us.
That is the basis upon which the Prime Minister now tells us the agreements arrived at in Ottawa have been effective. Let me read again a few words from what the right hon. gentleman said in London:
rl he basis of the proposal is adequate protection to the industries now existent or yet to be established.
That was the basis on which he made his proposals in England-the basis of adequate protection, the old Tory doctrine of protection.
He made his proposals on that basis alone, and he tells us that it is on that basis that the agreements now before us are made. In order that there may be no mistake in this I shall ask the Prime Minister to correct me if I am wrong. Speaking of my right hon. friend, I have said that from the beginning he was consistent in his attitude, that he believed in high tariffs with all his soul, and that it was only on a high tariff basis that he would make agreements with any country. He has done that; he has been following that policy consistently. I say however, when he tells us that the principle of protection is the basis of his agreements, when he tells us that this agreement is based on a policy of high tariffs and Canada first, he cannot expect us to give him support. In other words, he is asking the Liberal party of Canada to do with respect to its principles what he asked Great Britain to do with respect to her fiscal policy. He said to Great Britain, "You must change your fiscal policy before I will negotiate with you." He now says to us, "You must change your principles or you cannot support this agreement." The fiscal policy of Great Britain has been changed. Whether the right hon. gentleman was responsible for changing it is a matter of indifference; the fact remains that it has been changed. On this side of the house, we of the Liberal party still believe in^ the principle of greater freedom of trade. We do not accept the principle of protection, and we cannot be expected to accept as policies which may help this country or the empire, agreements which are avowedly based on protectionist policies, and particularly a protectionist policy of the type laid down by my right hon. friend at the conference of 1930, and which caused that conference to be the deplorable tragedy we know it was.
There can be no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that that is the view taken of the agreement. Perhaps I cannot do better than to run through the agreement clause by clause; that is at least the only way to appreciate what it is we are being asked to approve. I read article I:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom undertake that orders shall be made in accordance with the provisions of section 4 of the Import Duties Act, 1932, which will ensure the continuance after the 15th November, 1932, of entry free of duty into the United Kingdom of goods consigned from any part of the British Empire and grown, produced or manufactured in Canada which by virtue of that act are now free of duty subject,, however, to the reservation set forth in schedule A appended hereto.
In speaking of that article of the agreement the Prime Minister stated that this was a great gain, that the government had secured the continuance of the continued free entry of goods into the British market as a result of the conference. The Import Duties Act which was passed in February of this year imposed duties on a very large number of commodities, but commodities from the dominions were exempt until November 15 of this year. Undoubtedly that provision was placed in the act with the view of safeguarding the situation for the future, but does anyone suppose that the British government would have thought of later on imposing duties against the different dominions on the various articles that were exempted at the time the act was put into effect? The British government had already shown towards Canada an attitude similar to that Canada showed towards the British government when we granted the preference in our markets;
of its own volition it gave Canada free entry into the markets of Great Britain with respect to those commodities on which duties were imposed when coming from other countries but as of our own volition we gave our preferences to the United Kingdom. Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin, speaking in this very chamber, representing the British government, drew attention to the fact that this right of free duty to the British market was something which this country might well appreciate. Mr. Baldwin's whole plea at the beginning of the conference-and it represented the British point of view at the beginning, however it may have changed later on-was that the conference might result in the reduction of tariffs all round rather than in the raising of tariffs as between the different parts of the British Empire or against other countries. Then how can my right hon. friend claim that the conference won anything in that regard? As I say, we have been enjoying that market ever since February, and this is October. My Tight hon. friend says it is going to be a great thing for the manufacturers of this country to have that great market of forty million people in which to sell our Canadian products. May I say to the right hon. gentleman that if Canadian manufacturers are able to go into the British market and successfully compete I do not see that they need anything in the way of further protection against British industry in this market. My right hon. friend would have us believe the conference had given our manufacturers the right to sell their goods in the British market. I say that right was secured to us by the voluntary action of the British government months before the conference began its sittings.
More than that, the Canadian government was not the only government represented at the conference; all the other parts of the British Empire were represented as well. Is no credit to go to any other part of the empire for what may have been accomplished, if aught was accomplished, in the continuance of this freedom of entry into the British market? And may I ask further if it is to be assumed that Great Britain is desirous of declaring economic war against the dominions? That is exactly what would be happening if Great Britain began putting up tariff barriers against the entry of goods from the dominions. No; there were many reasons which governed Britain's action. One was that there are some people left in the United Kingdom who still believe in the wisdom of the free entry of goods, and there are many things they want to

Let me read schedule A:
As regards eggs, poultry, butter, cheese and other milk products, free entry for Canadian produce will be continued for three years certain. His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, however, reserve to themselves the right after the expiration of the three years, if they consider it necessary in the interests of the United Kingdom producer to do so, to review the basis of preference, so far as relates to the articles above enumerated, and, after notifying His Majesty's government in Canada either to impose a preferential duty on Canadian produce, whilst maintaining existing preferential margins, or, in consultation with the Canadian government, to bring such produce within any system which may be put into operation for the quantitative regulation of supplies from all sources in the United Kingdom market.
Do you see what that means? My right hon. friend says that it is very desirable that the agreements should be made for long terms. We have not him to thank that this agreement was not made for ten years. My hon. friends opposite have been saying that we -are going to be vastly helped by the agreement and that we shall have an opportunity now to sell our butter in the British market. They have not mentioned the fact that New Zealand gets exactly the same right as Canada in the British market, as do also Australia and the other dominions. They told

the Canadian people that we could not compete with New Zealand butter in our own market, and yet they declare now that we have gained tremendously by getting the right to compete with that same New Zealand butter in the British market. He said, "If you put your duties so high to begin with that we cannot get over them, the fact that you give us a preference does not amount to anything one way or the other." It has that right now.

My right hon. friend opposite ought to have groaned at the conference when the proposition was made.
That is not a correct interpretation.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce should have uttered his groans at the conference. This is another feature of this bargaining business; nobody is going to agree what the bargain was. This is the English language and some of us at least understand the meaning of plain English:
It is agreed that the duty on either wheat in grain, copper, zinc or lead as provided in this agreement may be removed if at any time empire producers of wheat in grain, copper, zinc and lead respectively, are unable-
Not merely unable.
-or unwilling to offer these commodities on first sale in the United Kingdom.

That is the first thing. They have to be offered on first sale. As I have said, if there is scarcity in other parts of the world, off goes the duty so far as Great Britain is concerned if any of our wheat producers begin to offer their grain for sale in other countries and are unwilling to offer their first sale in the British market. What is the next condition?
At prices not exceeding the world prices.
Where is the advantage that is now to be gained? We get the world prices now. That is all tlie Canadian wheat producer and the copper, zinc and lead producers are getting now, all they are going to get under this agreement; they are going to get the benefit of the world prices. Let us see how that works out. Let us take what will certainly occur. Canada sends her wheat into the British market. Other nations are not permitted to send their wheat into the British market while Canadian wheat is going in there. What are other nations going to do? Are they going to remain idle? Are they going to keep their wheat in their own bins? They will find in Europe some other centre which will become the world centre and they will ship their wheat there, with the result that there will be keener competition than ever at this world centre, and the world price of wheat will go down. Therefore the Canadian farmer will probably find, as I think the right hon. gentleman was told during the conference or as it was represented to him anyway during the conference,-that the effect of this provision may even be to reduce the price of wheat for our western producers. That is as plain as it can be. Supposing there is a scarcity in Great Britain, we have immediately to rush our wheat into the British market, but any advantage we might get out of the scarcity in Britain at present will be offset hereafter by the fact that the only price we can obtain for it is the world price if wheat be plentiful elsewhere. We have to take the world price for our wheat, no matter which way it goes. The Canadian wheat producer gets only the world price and what as a consequence of this provision may happen to be a depressed price. The same is true of copper, zinc and lead. While the farmer is getting less for his wheat, butter and a few other things and the door is closing against him in the British markets some three years hence for his dairy products, what is happening under this agreement to the necessaries of life he has to purchase and to his costs of production? When we come to study the tariff schedules we shall see that the duties have been put up to a higher figure with respect to commodities coming from outside the empire than they have been at any previous time, notwithstanding the enormous

United Kingdom
height at which the tariff stands at present, and the duties even under the preference are practically prohibitive, so that the farmer will have to pay more for his necessities and those things that affect the cost of production, and as a consequence he will get less for what he sells in the markets of the world. That is the agreement which hon. gentlemen opposite claim is going to be so beneficial to everybody, but five-sixths of the benefit of which is going to the farmers of this country.
May I ask my hon. friends this question because I think it is important. They maintain that they got a concession from Great Britain on this point. Does that mean that the British government undertook to increase those duties because of some pressure which was brought to bear upon them; that the British government did not wish to put them up, but that they were told in so many words: You will get no bargain and we shall not have any agreement with Great Britain except on the basis of preference, and if you do not tax the food of your people, we shall not bargain with you? Is that what was meant by getting a concession? If there was coercion of that kind, if that was the basis on which the agreement was made, the sooner the agreement is let fall to the ground the better, because there will never be any good come to the British Empire when what is arrived at between different parts of it in any agreement is reached as the result of coercion. There has been coercion in the past. There was military coercion for a long time. That was resented and we had about the last of it on this continent in 1776. For a long time there remained legislative coercion across the seas. That was put an end to fortunately by the Imperial conference of 1926, and what has since been enacted by the Statute of Westminster. Are we now to have something new in the nature of economic coercion? Is one part of the empire to be coerced into doing against its will in the matter of the taxes it imposes and the fiscal policy that is to govern, something that it -would not have done but for an endeavour to avoid a conference being a failure in the eyes of the world9 I say hon. gentlem n opposite will have to make pretty clear to this house and the country on what basis these concessions were arrived at. If the British ministers themselves were for putting these increased taxes on food, if that was all done voluntarily on the part of Great Britain, as in 1923 in regard to what was done there in a limited way, well and good, I do not think any of us should have anything to say 53719- is
about it. But if those duties on the food of the British people were put there as a result of pressure which the government of Canada put upon the British government, then no Canadian can escape the responsibility.
Some bon. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen may laugh, but I tell them in these days of suffering, taxes on food mean a great deal to the common people. We know what the cost of living is in this country, and with what difficulty people are living here. We know also that in the old country people are suffering from lack of food and of the wherewithal to purchase food, and I say if these duties are there as a result of pressure put upon the British government by hon. gentlemen, apposite, then this country is guilty of a very grave fault, guilty of a course of conduct which cannot be defended. Again I say, if it is not the result of a bargain, if it is simply the free will of the British ministry doing what they think the British people wish to have done, then there is nothing further to be said; but any attempt to coerce the British ministry with a view to bring about an agreement, however laudable the object may be, is wholly inr defensible and should not be supported in any parliament loving freedom and the right to manage its affairs in its own way.
Now may I take article 3:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom undertake that the general ad valorem duty of ten per cent imposed by section 1 of the Import Duties Act, 1932, on the foreign goods specified in schedule C shall not be reduced except with the consent of His Majesty's government in Canada.
I ask hon. members to note that article with great care. What is schedule C? Schedule C is timber, fish, salmon and other fish canned, asbestos, zinc and lead. I have already pointed out that as far as zinc and lead are concerned they are in the same category as wheat, the duty only remains as long as Canada is willing and able to sell in the first instance her supply to Great Britain, and so long as she sells it at the world price, otherwise the duty goes off. Now, as to timber, there is a small duty at the present time and that is being continued. That is practically all schedule C signifies as regard timbers. That leaves fish, canned salmon and other fish, and asbestos. In regard to fish I think it will be seen that the rates secured by this agreement are the rates that we secured voluntarily in 1923.

But the point of greatest significance in this article is this, and remember in endorsing an agreement we are above everything else endorsing the principles that underly it. This duty of ten per cent shall not be reduced except with the consent of His Majesty's government-where, in Great Britain? No, in Canada. This duty of ten per cent which is being put upon some of the food and other necessaries of the British people cannot be reduced except with the consent of the government of Canada. Can anyone defend an action of that kind? There is something very, very far-reaching and very significant. Let us turn the situation around; how would we in Canada feel if with respect to an agreement that had been entered into, our government, this Conservative government said, "We have fixed certain duties on timber, which has to do with all the work of construction, houses and the like, we have fixed certain duties on fish and other forms of food, and on copper and zinc, and we will not allow these duties to be changed except with the consent not of our own parliament but of the British government". How would we feel? Is there one member of this house who would support that? I venture to say there is not one hon. member in any of the parties who would support it. Then how can we ask the British government to support a measure which we in our own parliament would not be prepared to support if the situation were reversed?

Yes, under the kind of compulsion we have heard about, the government of the day in Britain has agreed to it. The British people have not agreed to it. May I add a further point that must not be lost sight of. This agreement is for the term of five years. In these premises, how can it longer be said that Great Britain has control over her own fiscal policy? How can it longer be said that Great Britain has the right to regulate her own taxes? It can-lot possibly be said that she has if this agreement is to remain in force, because here is a clause which says that only with the consent of the government of Canada can the British parliament lower the duties that have been imposed by this agreement upon its people in the particulars mentioned. Parliament in this dominion has struggled in the past for the right of self-government, for the right to control its own fiscal policies, and to have autonomous rights in all things; are members of parliament who have sought and helped to win these things, and have secured them

at the last with the goodwill and by the good grace of Great Britain, now going to try to fetter the fiscal liberty and parliamentary freedom of the people of the old land? Mr. Speaker, I say the principle embedded here is wholly indefensible and is undeserving of any support from any part of the British Empire.
As I have already said, this section has to be read in connection with article 22:
This agreement between His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom and His Majesty's government in Canada is to be regarded as coming into effect as from the date hereof (subject to the necessary legislative or other action being taken as soon as may be practicable hereafter). It shall remain in force for a period of five years, and if not denounced six months before the end of that period shall continue in force thereafter until a date six months after notice of denunciation has been given by either party.
May I point out that not only does this mean that by approving this agreement we abandon the principle of control of our own fiscal policy, but we surrender all right hereafter to protest about interference in the domestic affairs of our parliament or country by other parts of the British Empire; and we support another principle which is equally vicious, and which the Prime Minister himself has said is bad, namely we bind the hands of succeeding parliaments. What did my right hon. friend say in that regard? I quoted him the other day; he made it very clear what his view was as to binding the future of other parliaments. I have not his exact words at hand, but they were to the effect that any principle of that kind was entirely wrong, and he gave among other reasons why it was wrong, that it helped to create vested interests. Was he trying to create vested interests when he had that clause put into the agreement? Has he been trying, all through this agreement, to create vested interests, binding the people to a certain level of taxation for five years, was that for the purpose of strengthening vested interests in this country and Great Britain which exist at the present time? I am using his own words when I speak of the effect in the creation of vested interests by binding the hands of subsequent parliaments.
May I add this further, that there is no guarantee even as far as this clause and some other features of this agreement are concerned, that other parliaments in Great Britain are going to countenance this principle of having their hands bound by a previous administration. Indeed already some of the leaders in Great Britain have made very clear what their views on that point are. What does Mr. George

United, Kingdom
Lansbury, the leader of the Labour party in England, say with respect to these agreements in the event of the Labour party being returned to power?
Mr. George Lansbury, leader of the Labour party, speaking at Carlisle, said it would be a profound mistake if the statesmen gathered in Ottawa imagined that the present British government could bind the nation for a period of years to a policy of protection. The Labour party would never accept the principle of continuity either in foreign, dominion or domestic affairs. The Labour party wants, and will struggle for, international agreements which will enable the goods of the world to be exchanged fairly and equitably between the various nations. Tariff and preferences can never do this. The Labour party, whenever the election comes, will ask for a mandate to free the people from any economic entanglements which may be woven around them at Ottawa.
The Labour movement wanted the best of relations with the dominions, but these must be a part of the international relationships with the rest of the world.
There is a statement by the leader of the Labour party in England, and it is endorsed by Mr. Arthur Henderson, another leader of Labour, who in a letter denounced the British government for-

bartering away for years our freedom to determine our own fiscal system and making concessions which must be paid for by the British householder in higher prices.
I would also quote here, because they are entitled to speak for those they represent, the views of the Liberal ministers in Great Britain including Sir Herbert Samuel and Sir Archibald Sinclair as expressed in the joint letter of resignation which they issued, in which they declared they regarded the Ottawa agreements as-
-a danger to the best interests of the empire, a derogation from the powers of parliament, a barrier to removing restrictions on the world's trade; a burden upon the British people and a probable cause of increased unemployment and social unrest.
And those views were endorsed by the executive of the Liberal Federation in Great Britain. May I say that the Liberals in Great Britain are just as loyal and true citizens of the British Empire as any others, and no one in this parliament has the right to>
question the sincerity of anybody in this or any other part of the empire who gives expression to his own views with respect to these agreements.
May I draw attention to the words of the Right Hon. Philip Snowden. I confess, whatever opinions others may hold of him, that he is a man I wholeheartedly admire, a man who has the courage of his convictions regardless of what the cost may be in the attitude which the public may take towards him, 53719-181
a man who is prepared to make for his convictions all kinds of sacrifices. What did he say of the Ottawa agreements, and he did not say it without having profound reasons for the view he takes? He said:
The dominions are to dictate to us where we shall buy and where we shall not buy. The agreements have surrendered our fiscal autonomy and have handed over to the dominions control of British trade policy, reducing this country below the status of the dominions.
My colleague (Mr. Lapointe) has just handed me the Prime Minister's own words with respect to this binding of future parliaments. Speaking to a bill that was before the house in April, 1928, the present Prime Minister then said:
This particular bill is, I think, the one in which we endeavoured to apply, as something that should be observed generally in matters of this kind, the principle to which reference has been made. Personally I have held a very strong view for some considerable time as to the undesirability of any legislature or parliament tying the hands of succeeding legislatures or parliaments with respect to annual expenditure.
