If there is any single principle of self-government, surely it is that the people have control over taxation, and are in duty bound to review the taxes every year. May I say to my right hon. friend that a tariff is a tax, and he cannot get away from that no matter what he may say to the contrary. Every duty imposes a tax upon the people of the country.
Next comes Article 5 which reads:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom will invite parliament to pass the legislation necessary to modify the conditions at present governing the importation into the United Kingdom of live cattle from Canada on the lines already agreed upon in principle between themselves and His Majesty's government in Canada.
That is a matter that might be considered apart from the treaty altogether. I see my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Mullins) is listening as we speak about the removal of a cattle embargo. I think he has the view that he secured the removal of a cattle embargo himself, that it did not require any conference to do that. I have always thought that he had a part in it, although I think the largest credit is due to the late Hon. Peter Larkin, who was Canadian High Commissioner in London at the time the embargo was removed. However, cattle embargoes have been removed before and they may be removed again, but they can hardly be regarded as having a special place in an agreement of this kind.
I come now to Article 6, and I ask hon. members to see what they can make out of it in the way of definiteness. One of the faults of this whole agreement is the obscurity of the language in which it is couched, the uncertainly as to the meaning of the words and as to what their interpretation and application will be:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom declare that it is their intention to arrange as soon as possible after receiving the report of the commission now- sitting on the reorganization of the pig industry in the United Kingdom, for the quantitative regulation of the supplies of bacon and hams coming on to the United Kingdom market and undertake that in any legislation which they may submit to parliament for regulating the supplies of bacon and hams from all sources into the United Kingdom, provision will be made for free entry of Canadian bacon and hams of good quality up to a maximum of 2,500,000 ewt. per annum.
Does that really mean anything? It means that a commission is sitting and is going to report, and after its report the government may submit some measure to parliament, but it does not say that the measure will be submitted or that parliament will accept tho

measure if it is. It does not say what the measure -is going to be or when the legislation is to become operative or for how long it will remain in operation. There is nothing there that binds the British government to do anything for a term of five years. It says nothing as to the time at which this legislation is to come into force or as to the period during which it will remain in force. That is another of the great achievements secured by this agreement for the benefit of the agriculturists of this country.
Article 7 provides:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom wall invite parliament to pass legislation which will secure for a period of ten years from the date hereof to tobacco, consigned from any part of the British Empire and grown, produced or manufactured in Canada, the existing margin of preference over foreign tobacco, so long, however, as the duty on foreign unmanufactured tobacco does not fall below 2/01d. per lb., in which event the margin of preference shall be equal to tbe full duty.
What does that clause mean? It purports to be doing something for the tobacco growers for a period of ten years. Notice how insidious this whole business is. At one point the protection is for a period of three years, at another time for five years, and here the government have succeeded in working in something that might be thought to extend for ten years. They seek in this way to have the public mind grow accustomed to protection over a long period, but there is nothing in the clause itself which necessarily means that any duty will be retained for any length of time, or that it must necessarily be of any particular amount. The article rather suggests it may gradually vanish. Look at what it says:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom will invite parliament to pass legislation which will secure for a period of ten years . . . the existing margin of preference over foreign tobacco.
They have now an existing margin which the article says may go on for ten years, but only provided parliament does not change it which it apparently has the right to do. Change it?-in what way? "So long, however, as the duty on foreign unmanufactured tobacco does not fall below 2/0id. per lb." The margin is kept only so long as the duty against foreign tobacco remains at a little over two shillings per pound. If the British parliament decides to reduce that duty the margin of preference becomes equivalent to the full duty, and if the full duty is brought down by shilling or pence, the margin disappears and the rate applicable to British Empire grown tobacco also. Of what benefit will that article be to the

United Kingdom
tobacco growers? Who will as a consequence of this agreement begin extending his tobacco plantation in Canada in order to supply the British market when at any time the British government, if it sees fit, may reduce the duty on tobacco, bring it down to any point, or wipe it out altogether?
Let us consider the next article.
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom will invite the governments of the non-self-governing colonies and protectorates to accord to Canada any preference which may for the time being be accorded to any other part of the British empire, provided that this clause shall not extend to any preferences accorded by Northern Rhodesia to the Union of South Africa, Southern Rhodesia, and the territories of the South African High Commission. by virtue of the customs agreement of 1930; and further will invite the governments of the Colonies and protectorates shown in schedule D to accord to Canada new or additional preferences on the commodities and at the rates shown therein.
I have not time to go into that matter at the moment, but I invite the attention of the house to the fact that here is a new departure with respect to the whole matter of taxation of colonies and dependencies. Under this agreement the governments are making, so far as the countries of the rest of the world are concerned, a closed preserve of the dependencies and the colonies. Heretofore they have been free to trade with these colonies and dependencies. We on this continent as colonies, sought for years to get freedom of trade, and not to have the government of Britain impose duties for us. Under this agreement. however, we in this parliament who have fiscal freedom in these matters, are to sanction a course which states that whether they wish it or not, these dependencies and colonies in order to provide preferences to other parts of the Empire must have certain duties against the rest of the world imposed upon them. There is another principle which I do not believe we in this parliament ought to support for one minute. I shall not touch the larger issues raised, but it raises further far-reaching questions when we consider what other countries of the world are likely to think, those' countries which are not only being shut out of the markets of the British dominions and Great Britain herself, but shut out of the great colonial empire, as well, in consequence of the agreements. Those are matters which may well be very carefully considered.
Now we come to the so called concessions made by Canada. Here I think all people in Canada will experience a very great disappointment. I was very much inclined to believe that when we saw the agreements, we would see the British preference restored at
least to its level of two years ago. The preference itself has been greatly decreased since 1930 as we know, the actual rates of duties have been increased against Great Britain as well as against other countries. This agreement, far from restoring the old rates as they were at the time the present administration came into power, has fixed rates which are so high that in many cases I believe as the result there will be little in the way of trade.
Not only has it fixed rates very high as regards goods coming from Great Britain, but so far as goods from other parts of the world are concerned, this agreement raises tariff barriers still higher. Can any one imagine a government going the lengths to which this government has gone in actually making still higher against other countries of the world the very high duties which were imposed as a result of the special session of 1930, the regular session of 1931 and the additional taxation oif the last session when the excise taxes, which in reality are customs duties, were increased.
Article 9 of the agreement is as follows:
His Majesty's government in Canada will invite parliament to pass the legislation necessary to substitute for the duties of customs now leviable on the goods specified in schedule E the duties shown in that schedule, provided that nothing in this article shall preclude His Majesty's government in Canada from reducing the duties specified in the said schedule so long ns the margin of British preference shown in that schedule is preserved or from increasing the rates under the intermediate or general tariff set out in the said schedule.
Before I venture to attempt any analysis' of the schedule itself, may I direct the attention of the house to the part of this clause which in my view' is the most and very significant.
[DOT]-provided that nothing in this article shall preclude His Majesty's government in Canada from reducing the duties specified in the schedule, so long as the margin of British preference shown in that schedule is preserved.
I draw the attention of the house to the expression "so long as the margin of British preference shown in that schedule is preserved". That means that if this agreement is approved for the next five years the parliament of Canada cannot change certain of the duties imposed under the schedule; it means that this parliament of Canada cannot alter its own customs duties, except in a very restricted way either reduce or remove. If as happens throughout the schedule a number of commodities enjoying the British preference are made free coming into Canada, and the duties are sky-high as against all other countries, the sky-high margin of pre-

Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment I was referring to the various items in the schedule that is attached to the agreement and I expressed surprise, which I think will be general throughout Canada, that an examination of the different items should indicate that, instead of the tariff of Canada having been lowered by the agreement it has been very considerably increased; that even with respect to the British preference, the rates, instead of being at a figure which makes possible trade with Britain, are in many cases so high as to give reason to
believe there will be very little in the way of importations of some of the items referred to in the schedule.
I drew attention, however, to what appears to be, I think, the worst feature of the entire agreement, which is that we are being asked under its terms to maintain for a period of five years these, in many cases, exorbitantly high rates of duty. To appreciate what that really means one has to take into account the heights to which the tariff in this country had been raised before this agreement went into force at all, to consider the level at 'which the general tariff stands as compared with those of other countries. I venture to say there is not another country in the world that has a tariff anything like as high as is our general tariff. As we know, it was increased in some cases twenty per cent, fifty per cent, in others one hundred per cent, two hundred per cent, three hundred per cent, four hundred per cent over what the old tariff had been. Yet by this agreement there are cases where the general tariff is put higher still.
The feature that is all important for this parliament to consider is whether it is going to adopt the principle of allowing one government to say what the tariff of Canada must be for a given period of time irrespective of what the wishes of the electorate may be. Whether we are to be bound for a term of years to the high tariff rates which a government that may be in office one day and out of office shortly after, may fix. That is the most serious feature of all. When we consider that this is an effort to raise tariffs not only so far as Canada is concerned but so far as other parts of the British Empire are concerned against the rest of the world, this ironclad arrangement of high tariffs existing around the British Empire for a period of years becomes a rather serious international as well as national problem.
I have been taking up the various clauses of the agreement, and I have felt that in justice to hon. gentlemen opposite I should not omit any. For that reason I shall continue with just a comment or two in regard to the remaining clauses. Article 10 reads:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that protection by tariffs shall be afforded against United Kingdom products only to those industries which are reasonably assured of sound opportunities for success.
Note, Mr. Speaker, that in every one of the clauses that refers to duties, it is repeated that the principle governing is that of a protective tariff. All the way through we are dealing with protective tariffs and this clause repeats that principle. It undertakes that

protection by tariffs shall be afforded to what? This is the most surprising thing of all. When the Conservative party launched the national policy, the cry was that protection was for the purpose of safeguarding infant industries; it was to protect infant industries. Once those infant industries became strong enough to stand on their own legs and to compete reasonably with the industries of other countries, the protection the people were told would be removed. But the present administration goes the length of saying that the tariffs are not merely for infant industries, but that protection by tariffs shall be afforded to those industries which are reasonably assured of sound opportunities for success. Once an industry has reached the point that it is assured of sound opportunities for success so that it can compete in different parts of the world, then it is to have the protection which the government gives it by tariffs. As I have already said, the industries that are able to compete in the British markets themselves ought to be able, I think, to get along without the additional tariff protection which this agreement purports to give them.
Article 11 reads:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that during the currency of this agreement the tariff shall be based on the principle that protective duties shall not exceed such a level as will give the United Kingdom producers full opportunity of reasonable competition on the basis of the relative cost of economical and efficient production, provided that in the application of such principle special consideration shall be given to the case of industries not fully established.
In the clause that I read a moment ago it was the fully established industries that alone were to get special protection. In this clause it says that special consideration shall be given to the case of industries not fully established, so that while the one clause purports to look after only well established industries and to give them protection, the next clause gives special consideration to those that have not yet become established, and also stresses that the tariff is a protective tariff. Always what is given is protection, more protection. As to what this clause really means, I am afraid the government will have to explain. The terms are most ambiguous. Who is going to say what is "reasonaible competition"? I am sure that what would be "reasonable competition" in the minds of hon. gentlemen on this side of the house would not be "reasonable competition" in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite. Who is to determine what is signified by the phrase "relative cost"? What do the words "economical and efficient production" mean? And yet this is a

phrase which is used to indicate the -basis on which tariffs will be either given or withheld with respect to industries in this country. Who is to decide what is "reasonable competition," "relative cost," "economical and efficient production"? Possibly we shall get a little more light in another clause or two, but in the meantime I want to ask this question: What becomes -under this arrangement ,of any effort to have a tariff for revenue purposes? Tariff for revenue is ruled out altogether. Under this agreement all the tariffs we are fixing are being fixed on the principle of protection, not on that of a tariff for revenue. If a government in Canada wishes to have a tariff for revenue, it is precluded from doing so for the next five years. It is hard enough to raise revenue in this country at the present time, and a large proportion of the revenue that formerly came to the treasury on account of a tariff that had been framed in relation to revenue, is dried up by reason of the tariff having been raised to a point that makes revenue from this source very scarce. I shall be very much surprised if any appreciable numbers of members of this parliament are prepared to surrender through any arrangement made under an agreement of this kind, the right to raise revenue by tariff in times like the present when taxation, heaven knows, is difficult enough to raise. The Prime Minister in speaking of the whole matter summed up this phase in the following paragraph:
Under this agreement, Canada has in addition declared that it will give the United Kingdom producers full opportunity of reasonable competition on the basis of the relative costs of economical and efficient production, provided that in the application of such principle, special consideration should be given to the ease of industries not fully established. Pursuant to that undertaking, this government has increased the preferences in the manner I have just indicated,-
Notice how special consideration is to -be given industries not fully established; tariffs are to raised:
Pursuant to that undertaking, this government has increased the preferences in the manner I have just indicated-
That is, they have put up the tariff higher against other countries.
-and has furthermore agreed to cause the tariff board, authorized by act of parliament at its -last session, to review, at the request of the government of the United Kingdom, any item in our tariff schedule which it is claimed is out of keeping with the principle adopted.
The Prime Minister a sentence or two further on sets forth a governing rule which he says must be read in connection with this

United Kingdom
paragraph. My right hon. friend will say later that what his government has established is a competitive tariff, but understand the basis on which it is established:
The general rule governing our concessions to the United Kingdom is that we maintain a tariff, though a preferential one, against their products.
Elsewhere he said the tariff is based upon the principle of protection. That brings us to article 12, which relates to the tariff board:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake forthwith to constitute the tariff board for which provision is made in the Tariff Board Act, 1931.
The comment which I have to make on that particular clause is to ask my right hon. friend why is it we have had to wait until the British government requested that a tariff board should be constituted to have the tariff board constituted in this country?	If a
tariff board has any virtue in it, surely it should have been constituted before this, not at the instance of the government of another part of the empire but at the instance of this parliament. My right hon. friend put a bill through this house a year or two ago establishing such a board. He told us that it would have to be put through at that session, and he also said the commissioners must be appointed for a term of ten years, and took rather strong exception to the statement from this side of the house that those of us who were here would wait and see how the commissioners performed their functions before we would agree to their being kept in office any ten years. But nothing has been done. We have had tariff increases ever since the present administration has come into office, and a tariff board if it was to be of any service should have been consulted with respect to all these changes. But now, after the tariffs have been made sky-high in every direction, my right hon. friend comes along and says, " I will constitute the tariff board which I told parliament a year or two ago would be established in Canada." But established for whom? For the benefit of the Canadian consumer, the Canadian farmer, the people of this country? Not at all. Established for the purpose of enabling British manufacturers to appear before it to find out whether their interests are being sufficiently looked after. And this from the Prime Minister who went up and down this country during the last general election campaign talking about Canada first.
Now take the next clause, which relates also to the tariff board:
Article 13. His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that on the request of His
Majesty's government in the United Kingdom they will cause a review to be made by the tariff board as soon as practicable of the duties charged on any commodities specified in such request in accordance with the principles laid down in article 11 hereof and that after receipt of the report of the tariff board thereon such report shall be laid before parliament and parliament shall be invited to vary wherever necessary the tariff on such commodities of United Kingdom origin in such manner as to give effect to such principles.
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? It means that the tariff board of Canada is to be moved into action at the instance not of Canadians, not of consumers who are affected by our tariffs, not of any classes in this country, but at the instance of the British government. In other words we are to have a government of another part of the empire say when our tariff machinery is to be put into motion where it relates to matters pertaining to the tariff board. That comes back to the old question as to how far we want the affairs of this country interfered with by the governments of the other parts of the empire. I venture to say that if we are looking for trouble that is the best direction in which to seek it. If we are going to put upon the British government the onus of moving our tariff board into action, and put upon our own government the onus of having its board take up investigations whenever the British government wish to have an inquiry made, it seems to me we are going out of our way to make difficulties between the governments of the two countries and between the two countries themselves. May I also say that if the principle is sound, if the tariff board is in that way to perform a useful function with respect to the manufactures of Great Britain, why is it limited only to those who are shipping goods into this country from Great Britain? Why are exporters from other countries not equally entitled to appear before the tariff board and to be heard with respect to what the tariff is? The principle is either sound or it is not sound. Why should it be restricted in this fashion to the action of a government of another part of the empire and with respect to interests that are not Canadian but British?
But there is another feature which is even worse with respect to the tariff board. My right hon. friend said the tariff board was to have judicial functions. If anyone will read the speech Lord Hailsham made in Calgary he will find how far in the opinion of the British government this judicial function on the part of the tariff board was to extend. In so many words it was stated that hereafter, with respect to the matters referred to in this agreement, the tariff is to be a matter of concern not for the parliament of Canada and

the people's representatives in parliament, but for this judicial body that is being established in the form of a tariff board. That I say is a thoroughly unsound principle. Tariffs are a form of taxation; they are part of the fiscal policy of the country, and no government has a right to take away from parliament its full control over fiscal policy. Time and again the Tory party in Canada has sought in one way and another to have the tariff put up to a certain height and then kept there at the instance of some tribunal that was to have the whole say as to how it was to be varied. I venture to say that if my right hon. friend thinks he has met with success in that endeavour he is very much mistaken. I do not believe that any parliament of Canada will agree to surrender to any tariff board which is to be regarded as a judicial tribunal the say as to what the tariff in Canada is to be with respect to any commodity whatever. That right belongs to this House of Commons. The representatives of the people in parliament are the only ones who have a right to have any say with respect to the taxation the people of Canada have to bear, and will never endorse any other principle, no matter how beautiful may be the language in which it is couched, or whether it relates to an agreement between different parts of the empire rather than peculiarly and immediately to our own country.
What else does the agreement say in regard to the tariff board?
Article 14. His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that no existing duty shall be increased on United Kingdom goods except after an inquiry and the receipt of a report from the tariff board, and in accordance with the facts as found by that body.
Now I draw attention to the principle underlying that. The principle laid down there is that the tariff board must decide in the first instance what duties may be reduced and where they affect British commodities, that duties cannot be reduced at all until the tariff board so indicates. Well, again that is an entire surrender of our fiscal rights. I do not care whether it is a question of reducing or of increasing duties; the right belongs to this House of Commons to do both, and we can never agree to surrender to a judicial tribunal or any other kind of a tribunal the right to decide what the duties of Canada shall be.
I want to draw attention to this further fact, that a large section of the people of this countiy are not likely to have much confidence in any decisions which may be reached by a tariff board the personnel of which is

appointed by my right hon. friend opposite. Not that I do not think he will endeavour to get someone to cany out his intentions. I say it for this reason: He has declared already that the whole principle on which this trade agreement is to be carried out is the principle of protection, and he is going to get a tariff board for what purpose? To see that the principle of protection is maintained in the tariff. My right hon. friend asks us then to agree to his appointing gentlemen who will see that the principle of protection is maintained in our tariff for a period of at least ten years. He says that this board is to be appointed for ten years. He says that under this agreement their particular task is to see that the principle of protection is maintained. I wonder if all hon. gentlemen opposite are going to endorse wholeheartedly that particular idea. I say to them that they had better consider very carefully the people they are representing in this parliament, because at this time as never before the people will expect their representatives in parliament to speak out and say what they think is in the interests of the people. We have had tariffs increased to the point where they have brought exasperation to all classes in Canada -to importers, exporters, merchants, retailers, business men and consumers. There is not a class in this country that is not exasperated by the heights to which the tariff has been raised and the way in which it has been administered. Now we are being asked to keep the tariff at these heights and to take away from parliament and give to a judicial tribunal which my right hon. friend will appoint the task of seeing that that principle of protection is maintained in the tariff. It is a pretty serious business, I say, for hon. members to agree to any principle of that kind.
May I add this? Nothing is said in this agreement about the excise tax. While the clause states that the duties are not to be lowered except on the condition mentioned so far as the particular commodities referred to in this one section are concerned, it does not say that the government of Canada shall be precluded from increasing the excise tax on any commodity entering Canada from Great Britain or elsewhere. The session before last a one per cent excise tax was imposed on all commodities entering this country, and last session that was increased by two per cent, making the excise tax three per cent, and when you take into consideration the fact that the excise tax is imposed on top of the actual tariff as it is levied, in many oases it comes nearer to being a four

United Kingdom
per cent than a three per cent addition to the duty. There is nothing here which would prevent the government from adding another two or three or four per cent to the excise tax. They can just go on adding to the excise tax as they see fit, and thereby defeat altogether the whole purpose of the clause I have just read.
Article 15 reads:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that United Kingdom producers shall be entitled to full rights of audience before the tariff board when it has under consideration matters arising under Articles 13 and 14 hereof.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I need not draw attention again to the fact that here it is not the people of Canada that are thought of in this agreement. It is United Kingdom producers who are to have the right to appear before the tariff board. Why have not the producers of Canada and the consumers of Canada the right to appear before the board? May I remind the house in this connection of one important clause in the Tariff Board Act as it now stands, and that is that only those matters are to come 'before the tariff board which the Prime Minister wants to have placed before it.

I speak from experience to this extent, that I have never at any time asked that anything should be withheld from a tariff board.
Now we come to article 16, and may I say that the further we proceed with this agreement the more clearly we see that the things which it was impossible to have done by this administration at the instance of this parliament are now being done, if done at all, at the instance of other parts of the empire. Surely for a Canada first government that is an extraordinary position. We here in this House of Commons have been demanding and the people of Canada have been asking over and over again that there should be some stability in the tariff so that the people might
know where they stood in the matter of imports, that there should be an end to this making of tariffs by order in council and the alteration of tariffs by departmental regulation for the purposes of valuation in relation to exchange, dumping and what not besides! We have contended that under the present administration it is impossible for importers to know what the actual duties are likely to be by the time the present administration get through with their own valuations. It did not require any powers of prophecy to be able to discern that the first thing the British government would ask would be that there should be some stability about the Canadian tariff, that these irregular practices would have to end. And so it is not surprising to find the following clause in the agreement, though it is surprising that it should be inserted there by a Canada first government at the instance of the British government rather than at the instance of the parliament of Canada. Article 16 reads:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that customs administration in Canada shall be governed by such general principles as will ensure: (a) the avoidance, so far as reasonably possible, of uncertainty as to the amount of customs duties and other fiscal imposts payable on the arrival of goods in Canada; (b) the reduction of delay and friction to a minimum; and (c) the provision of machinery for the prompt and impartial settlement of disputes in matters appertaining to the application of tariffs.
Here at last is an admission on the part of this government that the sort of thing therein mentioned has been going on for the past two years, and the only reason this clause now appears is that the British government would not have anything to do with the government of Canada in the matter of a trade agreement unless they were given some assurance of this kind. Unfortunately there is no guarantee that the assurance will be carried out.
I need not emphasize the general nature of the language as to the particular machinery that is to be set up, and how and by whom it is to be administered, but I would say this to my hon.. friend the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman), that if it is left to him I do not expect that there will be much alteration.
There has not been much alteration in the administration since the right hon. gentleman was in power.
Potatoes are radishes now.

I thought my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue was awake.

Next comes article 17, which reads:
His Majesty's government in Canada undertake that all existing surcharges on imports from the United Kingdom shall be completely abolished as soon as the finances of Canada will allow. They further undertake to give sympathetic consideration to the possibility of reducing and ultimately abolishing the exchange dumping duty in so far as it applies to imports from the United Kingdom.
Does anybody believe that that means anything at all? It is another admission that the government have been doing things they should not have been doing, and that strong exception has been taken to their action by the British government, and there has been an effort made on the part of the Canadian government to make it appear that they are going to mend their ways. But if the principle enunciated here is a sound one, why may I ask is it confined to goods coming into this country from Great Britain? Why not apply the same principle to goods entering Canada from any part of the world? Are we to cease all trade with the rest of the world as soon as this agreement goes through? It begins to look like it. The more one studies what is designed by the various articles of the agreement, the more one comes to the conclusion that an effort is being made to have a great protectionist wall thrown around the British empire, and that matters are being so arranged as to make next to impossible hereafter extensive trade with any other part of the world. That is what I say it begins to look like. These clauses which restrict to Great Britain, the application of all the good intentions of the government, give reason to feel that there is a good deal of truth in that particular thought.
The next clause, article 18, is not one of any considerable importance; I do not think it will make any difference to the result whether or not it is approved. The article is as follows:
Article 18. His Majesty's government in Canada undertake to modify the existing regulations governing the importation of pedigree stock from the United Kingdom into Canada in a manner already agreed upon in principle, between themselves and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom.
As the matter has already been agreed upon, and the British government has undertaken to carry out its part, I have no doubt it will fulfil its promise, whether or not such promise is contained in an agreement.
Then, article 19 follows. We are now getting down to some of the small stuff, I am afraid. It sounds important enough.
Oh, oh.
Small stuff all along.

Article 19 is as follows:
Article 19. His Majesty's government in Canada undertake to accord to those non-selfgoverning colonies, protectorates and the mandated territories to which the benefits of the British preferential rates are at present accorded, and also to Zanzibar, the preferences on the commodities and at the rates shown in schedule F and also any preferences for the time being accorded to the United Kingdom. Provided that His Majesty's government in Canada shall not be bound to continue to accord any preferences to any colony or protectorate which, not being precluded by international obligations from according preferences, either (1) accords to Canada no preferences or (2) accords to some other part of the empire (in the case of Northern Rhodesia, except the Union of South Africa, Southern Rhodesia, and the territories of the South African High Commission) preferences not accorded to Canada.
I shall not attempt to interpret the meaning of that clause beyond reminding the house of urhat I said a little earlier in the day, that what is being done with respect to relations between these protectorates, colonies, mandated territories, and the like, in the way of giving exclusive privileges to parts of the British empire, and taking away from other parts of the world corresponding trading advantages which they had hitherto enjoyed, constitutes a very serious question.
The Prime Minister referred off and on to the Canada-West Indies trade agreement w'ith which article 20 of this agreement deals specifically. It is as follows:
Nothing in this agreement shall prejudice or diminish any of the benefits enjoyed by any of the parties thereto under the Canada-West Indies trade agreement dated the 6th July, 1925.
That agreement was drawn, as my right hon. friend has said, by a Liberal administration. I thank him and his friends for acknowledging the satisfactory nature of the agreement, which is indicated by its continuance. My hon. friend referred to a ten year period, and later stressed it in connection with the West Indies agreement.
A twelve year period.

indefinitely thereafter, subject to six months' notice. Now we come to trade agreements with a number of small countries, with which we exchange a relatively small number of articles. There is the convention of commerce with Belgium, the convention of commerce with Czechoslovakia, the convention of commerce with Italy, the convention of commerce with the Netherlands, and the trade agreement with the British West Indies. Omitting mention of the British West Indies agreement, with which I have already dealt, the other four-namely, the conventions with Belgium, Czechoslovakia, Italy and the Netherlands-comprise the only other treaties mentioned by the Prime Minister which run for periods longer than one year. They are in operation for four years. My right hon. friend states the present agreement will run for only five years. May I, however, draw attention to this important feature: There is no clause in any one of these agreements running for four years which compels this parliament to keep any portion of its duties at a certain figure for the period of time for which such agreements are in force. All the agreements do is to give the most favoured nation treatment to the particular countries affected. They leave this parliament perfectly free to alter the tariff as it thinks best. There is all the difference in the world between an agreement which runs for a period of years, but which leaves parliament free to act as it thinks best with regard to tariffs, and an agreement which is fixed for five years and which says that on many items

the governments concerned cannot alter its tariffs in that period of time, whether or not they may wish to do so. I think unquestionably the five year period is one of the most objectionable features of the agreement, but here again we have to thank others rather than the head of our own government for the fact that the agreement has not been fixed for a much longer period of time. Everyone knows that in the speech with which my right hon. friend opened the conference, he stressed the importance of having agreements arrived at for long periods of time. What happens in a case like that? You create vested interests, just as my right hon. friend has said; you enable those privileged groups to become more strongly entrenched, and when the agreement relates not merely to a country but to an empire you get some idea of the monopolies you are creating behind tariff barriers, especially in a country such as this. Nothing, Mr. Speaker, is more dangerous to the great body of the people of the British Empire than the combines and monopolies which have been and will be created under the terms of this agreement.
And the other dominions agreed to the same period of time.

And the other dominions, so far as I know, also had Tory governments. It is a Tory conspiracy. What have we had? We have had a number of governments coming together from different parts of the empire, all of them committed to protection, and drawing up a protectionist zollverein the like of which has not been attempted by any group of countries on the earth with the exception of those which comprised the German Empire. My hon. friends well know that that is what took place. These governments, committed to protection, all happening to be in power just at the same time, met here and drew up a series of agreements. Not satisfied with seeking to extend and maintain protection in their own countries for a long time they seek to have protection extend like some ring of iron around the British Empire as a whole.
There is one further clause, Mr. Speaker, with which I should like to deal; I refer to clause 23 of the agreement:
In the event of circumstances arising which, in the judgment of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom or of His Majesty's government in Canada, as the case may be, necessitate a variation in the terms of the agreement, the proposal to vary those terms shall form the subject of consultation between the two governments.

That means nothing, Mr. Speaker. It contains the words, "shall form the subject of consultation" and I should like to ask my right hon. friend this question: Under that section, in the event of a government in England wishing to end this agreement, and a government in Canada also wishing to end the agreement, would it be possible for those two governments to do so without violating any feature of the agreement or a principle that is fundamental? I wish the Prime Minister would tell us that. I think probably he will tell us that under this agreement, if we put it through, we are bound for five years, no matter what the people of Canada or the people of Great Britain may say with respect to what they wish to have done in regard to their tariffs during that period of time. I believe the Prime Minister will tell us that because of vested interests that are in the way of establishing themselves, I question very much if he will find, regardless of what he says, that governments will agree to continue what their people to whom they are responsible may insist to have changed.
That concludes my examination of the several articles of the agreement, Mr. Speaker. I have read every one of them. I have not omitted one, and I ask this house whether there is a single important clause in that whole agreement which does not violate some fundamental principle for which we in this parliament should have an abiding regard. I must say a few words, in regard to the form in which this matter is brought before parliament for approval. I spoke of the economic conference of 1923. That conference came to certain conclusions with respect to changes in the tariff which it was understood would be submitted to the parliament of one of them, but it left it quite open to the representatives of the people in the parliament of Great Britain to say what they wished to do in regard to the proposed changes. They were free to modify any of the suggested tariff items if they wished so to do. A list of items was mentioned in the agreement, but it was understood by the parliament of Great Britain, with respect to those items on which it was proposed to impose duties, that they had a perfect right to do as parliament wished to have done in the matter. Can we do anything like that at the present time? I ask my right hon. friend if I am not correct when I say that this agreement, in the form in which it is presented to this parliament, admits of no alteration in any particular. The tariff . schedules here, no matter how obnoxious they may be to any hon.

United Kingdom.
gentleman opposite-not to speak of those on this side of the house-cannot be altered in the slightest particular, unless I am very much mistaken. More than that, I very much doubt whether any amendment can be offered to this motion which my right hon. friend has placed on the order paper. Later I am going to ask his honour the Speaker to rule on that point so that we can be perfectly sure, but I think my right hon. friend has brought this agreement into parliament in the form in which it is, knowing that it is incapable oif being amended. We have to take this agreement as it is, every clause as I have read it, every item in the schedule attached to it as we see it, without the possibility of altering one single line thereof. If that is true, where is the freedom of this parliament? Whait real freedom have we, as representatives of the people in this parliament of Canada of influencing action as a result of discussion, opinion and argument? I repeat that the tariff changes mentioned in the schedule here are not something to come into force as a result of the judgment of this parliament. They are in force now and yet not a member of parliament has so far pronounced in favour of them, if we *except perhaps the Prime Minister. I doubt if there is one member of parliament who knows the full significance of any of these items, with the exception of the Prime Minister.
I am going to ask one thing of the Prime Minister, and in the reply that he gives we will have a test of his good faith in this regard. I ask him to allow these schedules to be discussed fully in committee of ways and means before we are asked to vote our approval of the agreement. I think that is a very reasonable request to make. We have facilitated the house going into committee of ways and -means; the committee has been established; the schedule is already before it and one item of the schedule has been called. It is quite within the power of the Prime Minister to adjourn this debate with respect to the main motion, and allow us to take up in committee of ways and means the various items set forth in the schedule. I ask the Prime Minister if he will give us that opportunity. I do not know whether or not he is prepared to answer that question immediately, but I wish he would do so. I say to him that it is a reasonable request to be made, and I say to him also that unless he concedes that right there is no member of this House of Commons who can possibly know what he is voting for when he supports the agreement. It is only when we go through the agreement 53718-19
item by item and see what is involved by way of increase or reduction of tariff, as compared with the tariff in 1930, or with what we think the tariff should be now, and when we know the value of the commodities that are going to be affected and to what extent they are going to be affected, that any of us can say intelligently what the agreement itself really means. We must remember that the schedules comprise the most important part of the agreement. So I say I hope my right hon. friend will give us that opportunity before he asks us to vote for the motion which he has placed on the order paper, calling for the approval of the treaty including the schedules.
Now there is one other thing. May I ask my right hon. friend whether these agreements can be amended, or whether his motion can be amended. This motion is to approve of the agreement. I know there are many hon. members in this house who would like very much to support certain features of this agreement.
Oh, oh.

I assume that some hon. gentlemen opposite wish to support the agreement. I am not surprised however, that they are beginning to change their minds. I assume that there are some members of this house who would like to support certain features of the agreement, but they would like to have an opportunity to make perfectly plain what particular features they wish to support. In the form however in which the motion is before us we are not without examination of the schedule in a position to vote intelligently upon it. There have been other agreements brought into this house in previous years which have had an effect on international relations, and when they have been brought in they have been brought in, in some instances at least, in a manner which enabled members of parliament to amend what in their judgment ought to be amended, and to approve of such parts as merited approval. One of the objectionable features of bargaining, however, and of arriving at an agreement as a result of bargaining rather than by means of voluntary action on the part of each parliament concerned, is that it involves either total acceptance or total rejection.
I am going to ask you, Mr. Speaker, to rule upon the question whether or not an amendment is in order. If it is in order, I understand that the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) would like to move
