May I say a word in conclusion with respect to one or two political and economic consequences of the agreement as it is .proposed?
We are told that this agreement is going to make for the .unity of the empire. In my view, Mr. Speaker, it is all-important for this house to consider how far an agreement of this kind will promote unity within the British Empire. My view is that unity within the British Empire is based upon freedom and not upon restrictions, and that this agreement, by increasing the number of restrictions to trade in many directions; by permitting interference in the domestic affairs of one part of the empire by another; by allowing interference with the fiscal policy of one section of the empire on the part of another; and by the misunderstandings which will arise over the interpretation of its various clauses, will1 go far to embarrass relations within the British Empire instead of creating harmony and good will among its component parts. That, in my opinion, is one of the reasons why we ought to consider very carefully whether this particular agreement should be adopted at this time. It is a very serious thing to take any step which will lead to friction between different parts of the empire. I think the British Empire suffered sufficient strain during the period of the conference itself. I -believe, as one distinguished writer has said, that we are perhaps better off that some agreement was reached than if none had been arrived at. On the other hand, as the same writer has said, perhaps the British Empire would have been much .better off if no conference had taken place. We ought, therefore, to consider very carefully whether these additional restraints on trade, which are being enacted by this particular measure, will help in any way towards furthering the unity of the British Empire.
Finally, there is the question of the effect of the agreement on world trade, which, I submit, is one of the most serious aspects of the whole situation. What this particular agreement does, considered along with others that have been drafted, is to create, just exactly as some of us feared, and mentioned at the last session, a sort of zollverein, a tax upon many commodities that come from out-

United Kingdom
side countries into any part of the British Empire. In case it should be thought that I am misinterpreting the views of the administration on this matter, let me quote once more, what I quoted the other day, from the statements of the Prime Minister. He spoke of the effect of this agreement in relation to the sort of policy that was being put into force. He himself has given a designation to what has been done by the conference when he states that it has created an imperial policy. I quote from Hansard:
I rather choose, at this anxious time in our country's history, to return thanks that the peoples of the empire-were able-to inaugurate an imperial tariff policy-
And elsewhere he has said:
If I interpret aright the attitude of this country to the great imperial policy we are adopting, public opinion throughout Canada would demand that it be so carried out.
And the essence of the great imperial policy is set forth in what he said, speaking at Calgary:
One thing was certain, however, that nations outside of the empire would be asked to pay some tribute for the privilege of trading within the empire.
There is a pronouncement of policy on the part of the administration, and I question very much whether it will appeal to hon. members of this house. Since when have we had imperial policies with respect to trade or any other questions determined for us in advance at an imperial conference? I have always understood that matters of policy were for the respective governments concerned. But here is a group of gentlemen, all members only of executives, who met together in conference in Ottawa and decided to settle imperial policy. We are told that what we have before us is a part of a settled imperial tariff policy, an imperial tariff policy based on the principle of protection. Well, since when has the constitution in the different parts of the British Empire been so altered that we have, meeting anywhere in the empire, a cabinet authorized to determine imperial policy? That is a new development, and, I say, a very serious one. It is a serious matter if, before parliaments have been consulted at all, before the people's representatives in the various parliaments of the British Empire have had an opportunity to express their views upon a great transaction such as the tariff that is to control for the next five years such a policy can be determined by executives brought together at a conference in any part of the empire. It is bad enough to have the tariff within one's own country determined merely by executive action without reference to par-
53719- 19i
liament; but to have a tariff policy for the British Empire as a whole laid down by the combined executives of the different parts of the empire is a new departure, and one which I venture to say should not be countenanced until authority of the parliaments themselves has been given to their executives to act in matters of this kind.
This is an endeavour to create a zollverein. It is an endeavour to make out of the British Empire an economic unit, something which many hon. gentlemen opposite think should be made out of the empire. What will be the result of the creation out of the British Empire of a great economic unit? That is worth pretty serious consideration.
Prior to the present time other countries of the world have felt free to trade with any part of the British Empire, feeling that they were dealing with autonomous self-governing countries whose affairs were controlled freely by their own parliaments. But hereafter if what the Prime Minister tells us is correct, the rest of the world will be told that there is an Imperial tariff policy which shuts all of them out from trade with the British Empire until they have paid tribute to the part of the British Empire with which they wish to trade, and this includes not only the self-governing portions of the empire but the whole colonial empire as well.
What Canada wants above everything else is markets. She wants markets within the British Empire, but she wants world markets as well. It is only as she gets world markets that she will be able to dispose of her surplus products in the different parts of the world. The British Empire itself, large as it is, cannot take all the surplus products of this country in respect to the total production of many of its basic industries. Can we suppose that other nations are going to look on with indifference at being thus shut out of the British Empire and allow Canada to trade with them as freely in the future as we have been trading with them in the past? If economic units can be created in one part of the world, they are certain pretty soon to be created in other parts. Already in all parts of the world we are beginning to hear talk of retaliation against the countries of the British Empire on the part of other countries. We hear rumors of its being made more and more difficult for the countries of the British Empire to find markets in other parts of the world, since other parts of the world are being shut out of the British markets. If such is to be the result, that, if nothing else, ought to have prevented this agreement from ever going into force.
292	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
Let me conclude by reading the words of Sir Arthur Salter, so often quoted as an authority by the right hon. gentleman opposite. They are words of one who has been giving close study to world economic questions and particularly those which relate to the tariffs of the nations. Sir Arthur Salter says:
If Ottawa has laid a foundation upon which more may he huilt, it has indicated very clearly that the limits to what may be built are much more restricted than at least English imperialists have believed. There were periods in the conference when the bonds of empire seemed very fragile-more fragile, indeed, than they are, for the temper and circumstances of the conference, the personalities of the delegates and of the representatives of the "interests" most in evidence, gave a distorted and misleading reflection of the real sentiments of the mass of the peoples in the empire. _
The strong and unanimous feeling toward the end that agreement must be reached was probably born more of fear than of hope-grave fear of what failure would mean rather than ambitious hopes as to the fruits of 6ucce6S. It is certainly true that the bonds of empire are stronger than if the conference had broken down. It is more doubtful whether they are stronger than if no conference had been held, and if the expectations which preceded it had never been raised.
The world as a whole will either move toward a system in which each country can exchange the products which it is best qualified to produce for those in respect of which other countries have corresponding advantages, or it will move toward an organization, national, imperial or regional, in which each unit will pursue the ideal of self-sufficiency, with their standard of living poorer for the I06S of world trade. . . We shall move as a whole to a world order in which each national unit will be a unit in the general commonwealth, or to a system of closed and, it may be feared, increasing by hostile units which will add immensely and incalculably to the risks of further wars.
Hon. gentlemen opposite at the Imperial economic conference had an opportunity such as has never before been given to public men in the British Empire. Their opportunity was greater even than that of those who came from other parts of the empire. They had an opportunity .to lead the way in helping to wipe out restrictions, to lower tariff barriers, to create greater freedom of trade within Canada, to create more in the way of freedom of trade throughout the British Empire, more in the way of freedom of trade throughout the world. They had it in their power to set to the rest of the world an example that would be helpful at the forthcoming economic conference whereby the world would find some relief from the thraldom into which it has come in this post-war period because of nationalist policies that have led to the putting up of tariff barriers by different countries and to the frustration of world trade. That was the opportunity they had. They failed in that

opportunity. Not only did they fail, but they have made trade immensely more difficult for the world hereafter. They have increased restrictions; they have raised barriers; they have made trade .more difficult in this country than it was before, more difficult as between different parts of the British Empire, more difficult as between the different countries of the world.
They had a still greater opportunity. They had an opportunity to further the great work of the League of Nations itself in seeking to promote peace and good-will among the nations of the world. They know very well that over and over again the declaration has come from Geneva that there can be no peace between the nations until these tariff barriers which are keeping them apart in t'he matter of trade, are considerably lowered or altogether removed. They had a chance to increase freedom of trade. They had a chance to advance peace and good-will among the nations of the world. In both of these tasks they have failed; both these opportunities they have lost. Instead of freedom and peace, their action was more in the direction of economic war. Where they have failed, where the great opportunities they had have been lost, the Liberal party of Canada will take up the task anew. It will take up the task of seeking to further freedom of trade between the different countries of the British Empire and between the British Empire and other portions of the earth; it will take up the task of seeking to advance peace and good-will among the nations of the world, this task it will take up with renewed energy and vigour; take it up with a determination to succeed where hon. gentlemen opposite have so lamentably failed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman has asked a question and I desire to answer it. The resolution which stands upon the order paper and which I moved the other day, is you will observe, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the fiscal changes consequent thereon. I apprehended that in the discussion the right hon. gentleman and his friends might take the view that has been taken, and those words that have been added, "subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the fiscal changes consequent thereon", involve the introduction of a bill by the Minister of Finance, and also involve the introduction of a bill in terms approving the agreement. The same thing applies in the case of Rhodesia, South Africa, and the Irish Free State. The resolution is framed in this form so as to meet

United, Kingdom
the tariff situation in accordance with the general practice that has prevailed in this country in connection with the coming into force of tariff changes and to meet the other matter as well, so that with the adoption of the resolution there will be not one bill but two founded upon it, one dealing purely with the matter of tariffs and the other approving of the agreement.

Mr. Speaker, we have listened to-day to a lengthy and exhaustive analysis of the trade treaty now in effect and now being discussed in the house. The rules of the house preclude me from entering into a discussion as lengthy as that of the right lion, gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King) who has just preceded me. However, if I am not able to give as lengthy and exhaustive an analysis of the trade treaties I hope to give to the subject at least a little breadth and I trust a little depth as well.
We have had, to-day, Mr. Speaker, a very important pronouncement on the part of the Liberal party. If I am to interpret what the right hon. leader of the opposition stated I would infer that at the first opportunity, when the Liberal party crosses the floor of the house and becomes the government of the country, they will abrogate the treaties that now are really in effect. I think I am not doing them an injustice by putting that interpretation on the remarks of the leader of the opposition. It seems that Imperial connections have been going, so to speak, to the highest bidder. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition has said that when his party comes into power they will give to Great Britain a preference of fifty per cent, basing that preference on the tariff that was effective when the Liberal party left office in the year 1930. When that statement was made there came to my mind the fact that in 1929 there was an amendment moved from this section of the house to the budget of that year. On March 14, 1929 the following subamendment was moved by my hon. friend the member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) and seconded by myself, to the amendment proposed by the party then in opposition, the party now in power:
That the amendment be amended by striking out all the words after "house" and substituting therefor the following:
"urges upon the government the consideration of an immediate and substantial increase of the British preference as a step towards freer trade relations between Canada and other nations."
As I look at the vote taken just a few weeks later, on April 11, 1929, I am almost ashamed to see among those who voted against the motion the present leader of the opposition.
However, what I want to point out is that when it comes to a question of giving rather extensive trade preferences, I am glad to see that the Liberal party are now following the principles laid down in 1929 by the little group to which I have the honour to belong.
I think generally speaking it is the opinion of all parties in this house that between the various component parts of the empire there should be the friendliest and olosest relationship possible. We in this corner of the house, just as in a general way the two larger parties in this house, are anxious to foster the closest possible relationships between the various members of the British commonwealth of nations- That commonwealth of nations occupy approximately one quarter of the globe and comprise about the same percentage of the world's population. There is no doubt that such a large population, about 445,000,000, can become a very powerful and important factor in the world's progress. Within its orbit we find all races and all creeds, and if these can be brought together to understand each other and live in harmony and peace we shall have accomplished far more than has been accomplished so far even by the League of Nations. I think we in the smaller group represented in this part of the house are anxious to foster that spirit of peace and good understanding with all sections and between all parts of the British empire.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to the conference of 1932. There is no doubt that this recent Imperial conference marks an epoch in the history of Imperial relationships. But I might ask this question, Is the general desire for closer relationships to be obtained by the method of increasing tariffs? I have no doubt that the government was imbued by the very best motives both at the time of calling the conference and during the conference itself. But when we look back over the past year or so to see whether trade treaties are desirable methods of cementing together the various parts of the empire, we are bound to feel a certain element of doubt. There immediately comes to my mind the fact that in the last year or two trade treaties have been abrogated, with much resulting friction. Once we enter into treaties as between one part of the empire and another and those treaties are abrogated, I believe the second condition is worse than the first; for in the first place by the creation of treaties we may be opening new avenues of trade, not necessarily increasing trade. That happened in relation to the trade agreements between Australia and New Zealand and Canada. And what was the result? After the treaties had been in effect
294	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
a certain length of time there arose a desire in Canada that they should be abrogated. This did not tend towards more harmonious relations. I think I can say the very reverse is true. Even today we have not overcome the difficulties and hard feelings that were created when the treaties were abrogated.
In the past the present government has looked upon trade as a form of war. I want to dissociate myself entirely from that viewpoint. In my opinion trade ought to be the cement that binds nation and nation together. As long as we have the viewpoint that trade is a form of war, any treaties we enter into are bound in the long run to be of no avail.
Will the trade treaties now before us, entered into at the Imperial conference, achieve the objective of drawing closer the relationship between the various parts of the empire? Why was the conference held at all? Was it because we in this country wanted a conference to be held for purely altruistic motives? Or was iib for purely materialistic considerations, that is, iconsiderations commercial in their character? I think I can safely say that the conference was called for the purpose of trying to create a certain diversion of trade into empire channels, trade that was formerly going to other parts of the world. I want to put on record some views given by other agencies as to what took place during the conference, and see whether what took place here really would bring about that much desired closer relationship. From newspaper reports at the time, it seems that the treaties that were being entered into were put on a purely business basis. Business considerations were the onlliy ones discussed. I find in n brief statement in the Daily Express of London, England, of August 20th, the following:
We have a picture of squalid squabbles with every big-hearted motive frustrated by the United Kingdom delegation.
Who was responsible for these "squalid squabbles"? This paper accused the United Kingdom delegation. According to this report, squalid squabbles " were going on in the conference room in regard to the treaties.
Then the London Daily Herald of August 19th:
The Canadian premier is now striving to win his end by forming a united dominions front against Great Britain.
I do not think that is bringing the empire together into closer relationship, assuming of course that the statement was correct. Then it goes on to say, " high tension still prevails." Walter Citrine and John Bromley, both of whom I happen to know, and neither of whom can be accused of being addicted to unduly 
strong language, were here officially representing the industrial labour movement of Great Britain. On returning to Great Britain they both made vigorous protests against the " sordid bargaining in which the British consumer has been a mere pawn in the food-taxers' game." That is what might be oalled the official view of the Labour movement in Great Britain of the conference that took place here.
In the London News Chronicle of August 20 last I find this:
One Dominion statesman said to me today with an air of melancholy, "I have come to the conclusion that the only way to prevent the break-up of the empire is to avoid conferences as you would the devil."
It seems at least that we have statesmen here in the Dominion of Chnada. In Great Britain we find that the national government has split over the conference agreement. Several members of the British government have resigned from office and the matter has become more or less a party controversy. The leader of the opposition in this house stated what was the viewpoint of the official opposition in the British House of Commons. He told the house that Mr. Lansbury had stated that if the Labour party were returned to power they would not be a party to an agreement which taxes the food of the gjreat masses of workers of Great Britain. In Australia the leader of the opposition, Mr. Seullin, within the last few weeks has made a statement very similar to that made by Mr. Lansbury in Great Britain. So I think that those who believe that empire trade treaties are a means of cementing the various parts of the British Empire into closer relationship are doomed to disappointment.
If treaties of this nature are to be binding, certainly they should not be of a partisan nature. Any party that is in power is bound to accept responsibility for its actions, but when it comes bo dealing with a matter of this kind, seeking to put into effect an agreement to be maintained for a period of years,
I believe such an agreement ought not to be partisan in character, but rather national, if such a thing is at all possible. I claim that these agreements entered into between the various parts of the empire are purely partisan, and because of that very fact I do not think they will live the length of time which their promoters intend that they should. It is doubtful if any more Imperial economic conferences will be held for a good many years, but if they are going to be held I think the party in power might well consider whether other sections of the house should not be

United, Kingdom
taken into consideration and even called into consultation when agreements of this nature are contemplated.
Why do I say that these agreements are partisan in their character? I turn for a moment to the remarks made by the Prime Minister last Wednesday when introducing these agreements to the house. What did he say?
They are based upon the principle enunciated by the Conservative party before the last general election.
When a party attempts to make an agreement of this character binding over a number of years, it is usurping a prerogative that does not belong to any party. If at another election the people of this country by an overwhelming vote decided that they did not wish these agreements to continue in effect, would it be right that after receiving a special mandate they could not abrogate them? I think that would be contrary to the best interests of Canada and subversive of parliamentary government. The Prime Minister has been good enough to state that these agreements are based upon the principle enunciated by the Conservative party in the last federal election. If I am not mistaken the important question in the last general election was not imperial preferences, but the economic condition throughout the country and particularly the question of unemployment, and it was largely on those two issues that the present government was returned to power.
And butter.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
If there were lingering doubts in the mind of any hon. member in this house or of any person in the country as to where the right hon. the leader of the

opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his followers stand in regard to these trade agreements, those doubts must have been cleared away today. Everyone will now be convinced that the right hon. gentleman and his party are irrevocably opposed to the agreements that have been presented to the house by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett).
The leader of the opposition spoke for upwards of three and a half hours, and I am sure the house will agree that it is impossible for one, in the brief space of forty minutes, to make adequate response to a dissertation of such length. Towards the end of his remarks the right hon. gentleman declared that the conference was a meeting of a Tory government representing Canada and Tory governments representing other parts of the empire, and that it constituted a Tory conspiracy which sought to rivet protection upon the empire. Those are the words the right hon. gentleman used. I took them down carefully at the time because I know that at times the right hon. gentleman, in a moment of enthusiasm, will indulge in language which later he endeavours to explain in some way. A Tory conspiracy on the part of Tory governments within the empire. Is the government of Mr. Forbes of New Zealand a Tory government? Is the government of Mr. Lyons of Australia a Tory government? Is the government of the Irish Free State a Tory government? Is the government of South Africa under Mr. Hertzog a Tory government? Is the government of Great Britain a Tory government?
Yes.

It is led by Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, but it is not a Tory government. It was not a group of Tory governments; the cold facts are there to show that it was not. Nor was there any conspiracy to rivet protection upon the empire. A genuine effort was made by the representatives of the governments of the British Empire to put into a practical form economic cooperation within the empire, thus strengthening the ties of sentiment and of constitution that bind the empire together.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Heaps) has very properly asked this question:	Are trade treaties the best
method of promoting empire solidarity? I do not quarrel with my hon. friend at all for propounding that question. It is a very proper question and one that might engage the attention of this house or of anybody that desired to discuss the matter in an academic way. But the point in the whole question seems to be entirely lost sight of by the leader of the opposition and many others

United Kingdom
who are critical of the conference. The point is this, that an effort has been made to do something practical towards improving the economic solidarity of the empire. Something practical has been attempted. We who attended that conference recognize that the full measure of success has not been attained, but we do believe that definite steps have been taken in the right direction. We believe that common sense agreements, practical and useful to all parts of the empire, and of mutual benefit all round, have been entered into, vphich will not only assist in the development of trade within the empire but will be a step forward in the direction of solving the various problems that are perplexing the world to-day.
The right hon. gentleman proceeded in his remarks to declare that Canada wants world markets. Of course Canada wants world markets. But the inference from my right hon. friend's words was this, that because Canada and the other dominions had achieved a measure of agreement with regard to their trade relations one with the other, therefore as a result of that they had shut out trade with other countries. It is not a fair conclusion. It was an inference to be drawn from the right hon. gentleman's words. He did not so declare, but he thundered it forth-*" What Canada wants is world markets." Of course Canada wants world markets, and Canada is striving to get world markets and will get them. Let me pause here to remind the right hon. gentleman of some of the difficulties that have been confronting Canada in securing world markets. All the implications of the right hon. gentleman's remarks, in the course of his speech of three or four hours, were to this effect, that Canada by its action at the Imperial conference, by its actions in this parliament in dealing with its tariffs, had to a degree dissociated itself from other countries in the matter of trade. He harps upon that. Well, let us see what the facts are. Does he realize that during the years that he was in office the leading countries of the world erected very serious barriers against Canadian products as against those from other sources? Are he and his followers aware that there has grown up, not during the last two years since we have been in power but during the last four or five or six years, a tendency towards isolation-in Europe a tendency to European isolation, a tendency to resist the inflow of goods? That step was taken by other countries before Canada did very much in that regard.
Let us take France, with whom we had an agreement entered into by the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues. In 1927, when the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues were in office, France increased the duty against wheat from 174 to 27 cents; and before they went out of office this duty was increased up to 85 cents per bushel-a prohibitive rate of duty. Take wheat flour; in the same country, I find they increased wheat flour, while my hon. friends opposite were in office, from 66 cents per 100 pounds to $2.28 per 100 pounds-again, a prohibitive tariff.

What did they do about
it?

Yes, as my hon. friend
from Lincoln asks, what did they do about it? Nothing at all. Again, take reapers: these were increased from 55 cents to $1.43; mowing machines from 55 cents to $1.47; fresh apples from 74 cents to 27 cents; condensed milk from $1.?5 to $1.53, and so on down the line affecting a whole series of articles. Turn to Germany. Wheat was free in 1925 and it had risen by a series of increases during the time my hon. friends opposite were in office, to 974 cents per bushel. The same applies to wheat flour; there was an increase from 86 cents per 100 pounds to $3.41. I have a long list of articles, so far as Germany is concerned, a full page of them-oats, for example, from 65 cents to $1.30; aluminum blocks from free to $2.75, and so forth. Take Italy. Wheat increased from free to 864 cents per bushel during the period hon. gentlemen were in office; flour from $1 per 100 pounds to $2.08; newsprint from 18 cents to 45 cents per 100 pounds; tires and tubes from $10.55 to $13.15 per 100 pounds; bacon from free to $1.30 per 100 pounds, and so forth. The same story applies to Belgium:	Cheese was increased from 30 to 91 cents per 100 pounds; wheat flour from 24 cents to 5 cents per 100 pounds; condensed milk from 76 cents to $1.26 per 100 pounds, and so on. The same thing is true with regard to Czechoslovakia.
The point I am coming at with my right hon. friend is this: While he was in office the markets of Europe were closing to Canadian goods such as wheat, wheat flour and various other primary products as well as manufactured goods. I am not saying that he is to blame for that, but I wish to point out to him that it does not behoove him to stand in his place in the house and suggest or throw
300	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
out the inference that because we are in office the markets of the world are being closed against us. As I have indicated by these quotations, they were in large degree closed before he left office.
He declares then that Canada desires and wants world markets, and that this agreement ought to be condemned and prevented from going into force because it will interfere with Canada's securing markets in other parts of the world. How he weeps, in his peroration, over the peace of the world! He says that the peace of the world is what he is after. Let me quote his words-"The Tories have failed, and where the Tories have failed the Liberals will take up the task of restoring once again the economic peace of the world." During all the time he was in office there is no evidence whatever that he suceeded in promoting peace throughout the world in any way, shape or form. There is no sign, no intimation, that by the treaties he put into force, all of which I have before me, there was any thought of or any attempt made to promote the peace of the world, nor was there anything done other than is done in this agreement. Every treaty he entered into was passed in the same way as is proposed in this case. Nevertheless he comes before parliament and says that this treaty with Great Britain must be accepted in full or rejected, and he says: "This is a terrible thing." I have before me the whole list of the treaties, some twenty in number, that have been entered into, most of them by the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues, and there is not one of them that was not presented to the house in precisely the same manner as this, to be accepted or rejected. Let us take the French treaty signed by his deskmate (Mr. Lapointe) and the late Mr. Fielding, whose signatures appear on the agreement which I have under my hand, by Mr. Poincare and one other on behalf of the French government and by a representative of the British government. It was signed in December 1922, with mo change possible in any item; and it contained page after page of items, far more than there are in this agreement. They brought it to the house in the following April and laid1 it on the table, looked us in the eye and said: "Take it or leave it." Parliament passed on it and accepted it, without being able to change one item. Yet my right hon. friend stands in his place to-night and says that the very foundation of this country is threatened by this agreement. I do not wdsh to be rude, but I want to teill the right hon. gentleman that when he indulges in that argument, as he did for a very considerable length of time, and repeats it, it is just pure claptrap, nothing 
else. Let us see what one of the leading Liberal papers in Canada yesterday had to say editorially on this subject. The Globe said-
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends have
been very glad to have the support of the Globe. The Globe said:
The Liberal opposition seem determined to attack the empire trade agreements in parliament. It is not clear that any useful purpose will be served by so doing and damage may result if it strengthens opposition in other countries.
And that is precisely what the right hon. gentleman hopes to bring about. He hopes, as was evident throughout every part of his speech, to stir up in Great Britain opposition to this agreement.
It is there now.

Yes, there is a certain
amount there now. The right hon. gentleman hopes to do this, because he knows for the last sixty, seventy or eighty years Britain had been in theory and in practice a free trade country and just now under existing circumstances they have parted from their historic policy. He knows there is still some doubt in the minds of many people in Great Britain as to the wisdom of doing so. He is seeking to stir up that opposition by trying to show that in this country there is strong opposition to this treaty. Why did he not move the amendment? He read it but he did not dare to present it to the house. Why? Because behind him-and I am looking at some now- are members who would not dare to stand in their places and vote against these agreements, members who in caucus-
Name them.

-have served notice on
their leader that in parliament they would not dare to oppose these agreements. The right hon. gentleman read the amendment. Was it really a courageous act to read the amendment, get its terms out to the public, and not move it? Why did he not move his amendment and give us an opportunity to analyse it, make a proper reply to it, vote upon it, and put the members of his party as well as of ours on record in the matter?
Then he turned to my right hon. leader, the Prime Minister of this country, and referred in bitter, somewhat scathing terms to his attitude in 1930. He kept reiterating the insinuation that the Prime Minister in 1930 in his attitude at the Imperial conference in Great Britain was lacking in proper regard

United, Kingdom
for the usual practice followed by statesmen in a conference of that kind. Let me tell the house what happened at the opening meeting of that 1930 conference. My colleagues the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) were present as well. This is what happened. The leader of the government of this country rose in his place as the premier of the senior dominion.
